#2840. Weekend Warm-up: Did Bayern Munich do the right thing in signing Jamal Musiala and Alphonso Davies to massive deals?

There is an uncomfortable question hanging over Bayern Munich's recent contract strategy — did the club make the right investments in Jamal Musiala and Alphonso Davies, or did it allow the fear of losing two exceptional talents to dictate financial decisions that could eventually become difficult to justify?

Both players received lucrative, long-term extensions in February 2025. At the time, Bayern Munich viewed them as essential building blocks for the future. Musiala was arguably the most exciting young attacking talent in German football, while Davies remained one of Europe's most sought-after left-backs. Losing either player, particularly on a free transfer, would have been a significant sporting and financial setback. At the time that each signed, it was reported that neither had a serious suitor.

But there was another consideration that could not be ignored — neither player had an entirely clean injury history. Bayern Munich was committing enormous money to two footballers whose availability had already become a recurring concern.

That concern has become considerably harder to dismiss since the contracts were signed. The numbers from Transfermarkt provide some perspective on why Bayern Munich's decision deserves scrutiny. Its seasonal injury-history summaries include both days unavailable and matches missed, although the records also include some non-injury absences, such as illness, quarantine, and fitness-related issues.

2026/27: 73 days missed, 3 injuries/ailments, 12 games missed

2025/26: 216 days missed, 3 injuries/ailments, 38 games missed

2024/25: 97 days missed, 3 injuries/ailments, 15 games missed

2023/24: 72 days missed, 6 injuries/ailments, 12 games missed

2022/23: 25 days missed, 4 injuries/ailments, 4 games missed

2021/22: 25 days missed, 4 injuries/ailments, 6 games missed

2020/21: 25 days missed, 2 injuries/ailments, 1 game missed

Musiala's injury record became increasingly concerning during his final two seasons before the new contract and immediately afterward. A hamstring injury in November 2023, recurring muscle problems, and a torn muscle bundle in April 2025 interrupted his progress. Then came the devastating broken fibula sustained at the Club World Cup in July 2025, which kept him out for 174 days and 31 matches.

2026/27: 5 days, 1 injury/ailment, 1 game missed

2025/26: 126 days, 5 injuries/ailments, 24 games missed

2024/25: 254 days, 3 injuries/ailments, 47 games missed

2023/24: 22 days, 1 injury/ailment, 4 games missed

2022/23: 71 days, 4 injuries/ailments, 10 games missed

2021/22: 140 days, 5 injuries/ailments, 27 games missed

2020/21: 47 days, 1 injury/ailment, 9 games missed

2018/19: 29 days, 1 injury/ailment, 8 games missed

Davies' record is arguably even more concerning in terms of cumulative absences. His 2021/22 season was interrupted by heart-related problems, while his 2024/25 campaign ended with an anterior cruciate ligament tear suffered on international duty. That injury alone cost him 221 days and 39 matches.

Davies subsequently experienced additional muscular problems, making his return to consistent availability another challenge.

These figures do not mean either player is destined to remain injury-prone. They do, however, demonstrate that Bayern Munich was not unaware of the availability risks when it committed to these contracts. In Davies's case, the question about investing that much into the left-back position for a player with that kind of injury track record is likely causing a lot of internal Monday-morning quarterbacking.

The reported salaries make the debate considerably more interesting. According to Sport Bild, the estimated annual salaries for the two players are listed below:

Musiala: More than €25 million per year, including potential bonuses. Per Capology, Musiala's potential bonuses total €12,450,000.

Davies: Up to €20 million per year, including potential bonuses. Per Capology, Davies' potential bonuses total €5,000,000.

Those are reported figures, not officially disclosed salaries. There is also a distinction between base salary and performance-related compensation. Capology, which publishes estimated salary data, currently puts Musiala's gross fixed annual salary at approximately €22.83 million and Davies's at €15 million, excluding bonuses. As you can see, there are some discrepancies because figures are not publicly released as you might see in North American sports.

That distinction between salary and total financial package matters. The headline figures are not necessarily guaranteed annual payments, and performance incentives can make a significant difference. Some recent salary coverage also suggests Musiala's maximum compensation is linked to playing-time thresholds. The exact contractual structure has not been officially confirmed.

There is another particularly interesting detail from the latest Sport Bild reporting (via @iMiaSanMia) — both players reportedly negotiated special provisions for continued salary payments during extended injury absences. Musiala's protection allegedly extends to six months, while Davies's is reportedly limited to three or four months. Bayern is also said to have taken out additional insurance to mitigate the financial exposure.

In other words, Bayern was not simply agreeing to pay two players enormous salaries. It was reportedly agreeing to additional financial protection even if injuries kept them away from the pitch for extended periods.

There is a very good argument that Bayern could not afford to lose either player in 2025.

Musiala was 21, already a Germany international, and had developed into one of Europe's most exciting attacking midfielders. He was producing goals, assists, and moments of individual brilliance while becoming increasingly central to Bayern's identity. He was also approaching the final year of his previous contract.

The danger of allowing a player of that caliber to enter the final year of his deal without an extension was obvious. Premier League and La Liga clubs were interested, and Bayern risked either losing him for nothing or being forced into a sale on unfavorable terms.

The BBC reported that Musiala had been granted a release clause as part of his new agreement, but the overall decision to retain him was understandable. Bayern needed a player around whom it could build its next generation.

Davies presented a different but equally difficult situation.

At 24, he was an established Champions League winner with extraordinary pace, athleticism, and experience at the highest level. He was also attracting considerable interest from elsewhere, particularly Real Madrid, and was approaching the end of his existing contract.

Losing a player of his quality without receiving a transfer fee would have been a significant blow. Finding a comparable replacement would also have required a substantial investment.

Bayern Munich ultimately secured both players through 2030. That gave the club long-term security, protected the value of two important assets, and avoided the possibility of watching them leave for nothing.

There was also a symbolic component. Bayern wanted to demonstrate that it could compete financially with Europe's wealthiest clubs and retain its most valuable young players. Letting Musiala or Davies walk would have sent precisely the wrong message.

The strongest argument against the contracts is not that Musiala and Davies were undeserving of significant pay raises. Both had demonstrated their value. It is that Bayern may have negotiated as though retaining them was more important than protecting the club against foreseeable risks.

Musiala's talent was never in question, but his availability was already becoming an issue. His muscular problems during 2023/24 and 2024/25 should have prompted serious consideration of how much guaranteed money Bayern was willing to commit.

Davies had an even longer history of interruptions, including the heart-related problems in 2022 and subsequent muscular injuries. Bayern knew it was investing in a player whose availability had been inconsistent.

There is a difference between paying a premium for exceptional ability and paying a premium without adequately accounting for the possibility that the player cannot consistently deliver that ability.

The reported injury-protection clauses make this especially interesting. They suggest the club recognized the risks during negotiations but was nevertheless willing to accept additional financial obligations to secure the signatures.

There are also broader concerns about Bayern's wage structure. Reports in 2025 and 2026 have described internal criticism of Max Eberl's negotiating approach, with some supervisory board members reportedly believing that the club was too accommodating and agreeing to unnecessarily expensive contracts. Musiala and Davies have been among the examples cited.

That criticism becomes more understandable when considering how many other players have subsequently received substantial extensions or entered the highest salary brackets.

Bayern Munich cannot have every important player earning €15–25 million annually without creating significant pressure elsewhere in the squad. It also makes future negotiations with players such as Michael Olise considerably more complicated.

There is, however, a danger in judging these decisions exclusively through the lens of injuries that occurred afterward.

Bayern did not sign two ordinary squad players. It secured two footballers with the potential to define the club's next generation.

Musiala offers qualities that are exceptionally difficult to replace. His dribbling, creativity, ability to operate between the lines, and capacity to produce something from nothing make him a unique attacking weapon. When healthy, he changes the way Bayern plays.

Davies provides a similarly unusual profile. His speed, ability to recover defensively, and willingness to attack space give Bayern tactical options that few left-backs can offer.

Replacing either player would have been expensive, and there was no guarantee a replacement would deliver comparable performances.

There is also an important distinction between an injury being unfortunate and a club making an inherently bad investment. Musiala's broken fibula and Davies's ACL injury were serious setbacks, but neither could have been predicted with certainty when the contracts were negotiated.

Furthermore, both contracts run until 2030. Bayern is not evaluating these investments over a single season. There is still considerable time for both players to deliver the returns the club anticipated.

The question is whether they can establish the consistency required to justify those commitments.

One could argue that Bayern Munich was right to prioritize retaining Musiala and Davies. Allowing either to leave in 2025 would have created enormous sporting problems and potentially cost the club even more money in replacement transfers.

However, there is a legitimate argument that FC Bayern also overpaid, particularly when considering the players' existing injury histories and the additional protections reportedly negotiated into their contracts — plus the fact that neither might have had an actual suitor pursuing them.

Musiala earning more than €25 million annually is a massive commitment for a player who has struggled to maintain uninterrupted fitness. Davies earning up to €20 million is similarly difficult to justify if his availability continues to fluctuate. Due to questions about Davies's ability to stay healthy, Bayern Munich also had to acquire a high-end backup in Nathaniel Brown, who did not come cheap.

The important distinction is that neither contract was necessarily a mistake when signed. The danger is that Bayern Munich may have underestimated how much availability would influence their value.

Ultimately, these decisions will be judged by what happens between now and 2030. If Musiala becomes the world-class centerpiece Bayern Munich believes he can be and Davies returns to being a consistently available elite left-back, the investment will look considerably more sensible.

If the injuries continue, however, Bayern Munich could find itself paying superstar money for players who cannot consistently provide superstar performances. The point remains — Bayern Munich was probably right to keep both players. Whether it was right to pay quite so much to do it is an entirely different question.

The late '90s was a somewhat odd period for music.

Grunge was on its way out, heavy metal was around but not thriving, hair metal was dead, and alternative was morphing into a bunch of different sounds. Somehow, Deftones was melding them all together and, in some cases, probably influencing a burgeoning emo movement as well.

This song was not necessarily a major hit or anything, but it did represent a look into the sound that was about to emerge in rock music in the early aughts. Enjoy:

The '90s classic Kingpin is getting a sequel — and this time it really might be happening.

While the project has been bandied about for years, it looks like it will come to fruition this time. During an appearance on The Dan Patrick Show on Thursday, director Peter Farrelly confirmed that the project was moving forward, but offered very little else on it. Peter would be reuniting with his brother Bobby for this project, as they worked on the original together.

Kingpin, of course, was a slapstick, somewhat dark comedy about bowling, a couple of degenerate pro bowlers, an Amish fella, and a lot of hijinks. The plot revolves around a washed-up former bowling prodigy who tries to reclaim his glory by mentoring a naive Amish prodigy.

In 1979, rising bowling star Roy Munson (Woody Harrelson) is hustled by his rival, Ernie "Big Ern" McCracken (Bill Murray), leading to a confrontation where Roy loses his right hand. Seventeen years later, a down-on-his-luck Roy discovers Ishmael Boorg (Randy Quaid), a sheltered Amish man with an extraordinary natural talent for bowling. Roy convinces Ishmael to leave his community and enter a $1 million tournament in Reno, Nevada, hoping the prize money will save Ishmael's family farm — and revive Roy's career — if they can beat Big Ern along the way.

Naturally, the biggest question about the sequel is whether the original cast members will return (which is not a certainty). There have not been any announcements on that as of yet.

One note on the original Kingpin is that it had a cool soundtrack (in the same vein as another underrated soundtrack, Dumb & Dumber).

Bayern Munich is not operating at 100% capacity, but it will still put out a very strong lineup. The feeling here is that the new grass at the Allianz Arena is going to get broken in with a few goals for the home team and a clean sheet.

#2838. Observations after Sixers come back for strong shorthanded victory

Observations after Sixers come back for strong shorthanded victory originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stretched their winning streak to four games and snagged a strong road win Wednesday night over the Magic.

They earned a 121-116 victory in Orlando to improve to 13-3 on the season. The Magic dropped to 6-8.

Joel Embiid had 26 points, seven assists, six rebounds, three blocks and two steals.

VJ Edgecombe posted a season-high 24 points, eight boards and six assists.

LeBron James scored 22 points and Anfernee Simons added 18.

Magic star Franz Wagner had 27 points, 11 assists and eight rebounds.

The Sixers had a long injury list in Orlando. Tyrese Maxey (right foot soreness), Jaylen Brown (left hamstring strain) and Dean Wade (left hamstring soreness/tightness) were among their players out. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse told reporters in Orlando that Brown will be re-evaluated when the team returns to Philadelphia.

Orlando was without star forward Paolo Banchero (right high ankle sprain).

The Sixers will start a three-game homestand when they face the Bucks on Saturday afternoon. Here are observations on their win over the Magic:

The Sixers' undermanned starting lineup was Edgecombe, Simons, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, James and Embiid.

After scoring 37 points in the Sixers' win over the Nets, Embiid had a subpar start. He began 1 for 6 from the floor and committed a turnover that led to an Anthony Black dunk.

The Sixers' lineup looked exactly like a unit that hadn't built any chemistry yet. The team was not sharp early on either end of the floor.

Desmond Bane drained a long three-pointer to give Orlando a 27-12 advantage. Orlando made 11 of its first 14 field goals and led by as many as 17 points in the first quarter.

Labaron Philon Jr. and Justin Edwards joined the Sixers' rotation. So did two-way contract players Tacko Fall and Caleb Love.

Philon impressed in the first quarter, converting two floaters and a corner three. The rookie passed his previous NBA scoring high of five points and finished the night with 10 on 4-for-5 shooting.

Fall played 10 minutes and posted two points, three rebounds and three blocks. He slammed in a dunk and rejected two shots early in the second quarter. Credit to Fall for giving the Sixers a good backup center performance and doing his job as a rim-protecting ultra-big man.

Love entered in the second quarter and was ready to fire, hitting a catch-and-shoot three-pointer on his first touch.

The Sixers' zone defense also helped them eat into the Magic's lead. The zone seemed to disrupt Orlando's offensive rhythm and it was active enough to prevent the Magic from consistently creating high-quality looks.

Edgecombe's buzzer-beating mid-range jumper cut the Sixers' deficit to 69-64 after two quarters.

The Sixers pulled within a single point on multiple occasions in the third quarter, including on a Philon three late in the period. They trailed by five points after the third.

Fall continued to play well early in the fourth quarter. He deterred the Magic's drivers from getting all the way to the rim as the very large back line of the Sixers' zone defense and made eye-catching hustle plays on both sides of the ball.

The Sixers outscored Orlando by seven points on the night with Fall on the court. Soon after Embiid subbed back in, he evened the game at 104-all with two free throws. Jabari Walker swished a three to finally push the Sixers in front.

The Magic regained a late lead with a Jalen Suggs three. James then drove and kicked the ball out to Edgecombe, who nailed one of his customary clutch jumpers to put the Sixers back on top.

No matter the night-to-night personnel, the Sixers have been fantastic at the tail end of close games. They're now 11-0 in clutch situations, which the NBA defines as games within a five-point differential in the final five minutes.

Keelon Russell didn't play a snap for Alabama football in its 47-0 win against Chattanooga. Austin Mack, Jett Thomalla and John Gazzaniga did the work at quarterback for the Crimson Tide.

Russell had three touchdown passes in Alabama's 21-6 win against Vanderbilt, completing 22 of 33 pass attempts for 217 yards.

#2835. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

#2830. Walker Kessler's first three-pointer as a Laker sparks resurgent second half

Lakers coaches didn't know why Walker Kessler was standing in the corner. But when Collin Sexton flung the ball to the center standing behind the three-point arc on the Lakers' first possession of the fourth quarter, Kessler knew what he was going to do with it.

"I'm confident in that shot," Kessler said with a smirk.

The 7-foot-2 center's strong second half sparked the Lakers' gritty 106-104 win over the Sacramento Kings on Friday at Crypto.com Arena. After Lakers coach JJ Redick "lit [him] up" at halftime, Kessler responded by scoring nine of his 15 points and grabbing six of his seven total rebounds after the break and draining the unexpected long-distance shot that put the Lakers up by one early in the fourth quarter.

Redick said the play, with the Lakers (14-3) trailing by two to start the fourth quarter, was a little unorganized, leading to their center somehow standing in the corner. Kessler, who hadn't attempted a three all season and was 17 for 64 from three-point range during four seasons with the Utah Jazz, took instruction from Sexton to space to the corner instead of slash to the rim. Sexton whipped a one-handed pass over his head to Kessler, who methodically rose up over Dylan Cardwell's late closeout.

Redick told Kessler once during the preseason after a particular timeout that if the ball found him on a called play and it wasn't for a layup, the center should still shoot. Although Kessler has faith from the coaches and works on his jump shot, Redick isn't anointing the 25-year-old an official stretch five. His teammates don't mind.

"I mean, if he shoots it like that, I'll keep finding him," guard Quentin Grimes said with a laugh. "If he's going to keep cashing it all net, I want more of them. Keep shooting."

Read more: Quentin Grimes' late three-pointer lifts Lakers to narrow win over Kings

Kessler's go-ahead three-pointer highlighted the Lakers' comeback from an 11-point deficit with 11:25 remaining in the third. During a homestand that appeared to be favorable but has turned into a difficult slog, the Lakers have relied on unexpected characters to star in big moments.

Grimes hit back-to-back three-pointers in the fourth quarter against the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday to fuel his career-high 47 points. The Lakers staged most of their 18-point comeback during the beginning of the fourth quarter when superstar Luka Doncic was on the bench. They trailed by 13 at the end of the third quarter. When Doncic subbed back in with 6:54 remaining, the Lakers, playing the majority of the stretch with two-way center Carson Cooper, were down by only four.

Cooper was playing the critical minutes because Kessler missed the game with lower right leg soreness. With Kessler back against the Kings (1-14), the Lakers repeated their fourth-quarter heroics, turning a two-point deficit after three quarters into a seven-point lead by the time Doncic returned.

Coaches made small rotational changes to the unit Friday, opting to start the fourth with Kessler, Sexton, Grimes, Matisse Thybulle and Jake LaRavia. Forward Sandro Mamukelashvili previously started the fourth quarter in recent games with Austin Reaves sidelined. Still feeling out the best lineups for the team, Redick said the exact groupings are "going to be a process."

The Lakers aren't fazed by the adjustments.

"I think we have a lot of heart and our ability to just make things work," said Thybulle, who had 14 points and four made three-pointers Friday. "We've been throwing out a whole bunch of different lineups. … Just being able to be adaptable, I think, has been a huge thing for everyone on the roster."

Lakers center Walker Kessler scores off an offensive rebound in the first half against the Sacramento Kings on Friday. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

The Lakers are 6-1 in the last seven games in which Doncic or Reaves have missed time. The superstars have only played three quarters of a game together in the last seven games. Doncic missed the game at Detroit with lower back soreness, and Reaves, who was sick in Atlanta on Nov. 9, has missed the last four games with a left heel bruise. The Lakers hope to have him back by at least next Friday on the road against San Antonio.

Kessler was sidelined against Charlotte for the first time this season. Like the rest of his teammates, he struggled against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, finishing with the quietest 10-point, 11-rebound double-double imaginable. He was in danger of fading into the background again against Sacramento before Redick jolted the team awake at halftime.

"I wasn't playing physical," Kessler said. "I wasn't going up to dunk the ball. I was missing some more touches around the rim. And then defensively, being undisciplined. Jumping at stuff I don't need to jump at. He definitely lit into me. It was good. I needed it. That's what makes a good coach. Knowing when guys need that and when guys don't."

While Redick said afterward he believed he was able to regulate his emotions during his halftime talk to the team, Doncic, who finished with 25 points and eight assists, characterized it more plainly.

"He yells," Doncic said. "But I'm used to it."

Kessler, a centerpiece for a franchise with championship expectations, is getting used to the demands of this new spotlight. He dazzled with 48 points in his first two games in which he made 22 of 26 shots, including 10 dunks in his perfect debut. But coaches demanded more production from his rebounding and fans are unrelenting in their calls for more.

"I know obviously you're on a bigger stage and stuff like that, but my teammates and coaching staff have done a really good job of picking everyone up even though we're struggling or we were struggling these past two games," Kessler said. "I'm not really focused too much on the outside but I understand that the L.A. fans expect a certain kind of performance. And I think it's not just making shots, but playing with effort and energy and I can completely respect that."

When Kessler goes to the bench, he hears jeers from fans imploring him to play harder.

When he hit that three from the corner, he heard some of the loudest cheers of the night.

#2829. ESPN is overreacting to Puka Nacua’s injury

Puka Nacua's career with the Los Angeles Rams has "probably ended", according to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler. But that report feels speculative, uninformed, and flat-out ignorant by Fowler.

The Rams will let Nacua leave in free agency? That seems ridiculously unlikely. Players of Nacua's age and ability are rarely allowed to hit free agency and no matter what the situation is on Puka's side or L.A.'s side with a long list of free agents and needs, the Rams would sooner franchise tag the receiver than let him walk for a third-round compensatory pick in 2028.

Nacua is worth at least two first-round picks, and the Rams know it.

"Up in the air as it pertains to his future with the Rams. Going into free agency, he has two significant injuries, including an MCL injury that Sean McVay says will keep him out a few months ago. Probably ends his tenure with the Rams," says Fowler.

Jeremy Fowler is typically a solid reporter, so it's hard to fathom why he would go to the lengths of saying that Nacua's career with the Rams is "probably over" while in the next breath acknowledging that Nacua is the best free agent of 2027.

The "best free agent" next year is never a free agent.

Although the Rams have challenging test ahead for Les Snead when it comes to their free agents and budget, keeping Nacua — or at least tagging him — is non-negotiable. Snead will not let Nacua leave "in free agency" like Fowler says under any circumstances, unless pigs fly by March.

The only rational way that Nacua's career ends is if the Rams tag him and he is traded for at least a first and a second-round pick, if not better. That will also be tough for L.A. to manage given the complexity of trades of that magnitude and the need to find a team that is not only willing to pay Nacua like a top-tier receiver, but also sacrifice the draft picks to complete a deal.

Hypothetically let's say that the Raiders want to trade for Nacua and Las Vegas is holding pick 10. Will the Raiders be willing to trade pick 10 and pick 42 and pay Nacua a four-year, $170 million contract? If there's any team willing to do that it would be the Raiders, but Las Vegas is under new management and Tom Brady may not be so quick to rush a deal like that for Nacua.

As bad as things look now, the fact is that Nacua is the best player on the Rams and this is a roster that is about to get a whole lot less talented in 2027 if Matthew Stafford and Davante Adams and Aaron Donald retire/walk away.

What star power is left? Ty Simpson and Konata Mumpfield?

Unless the Rams want to do a full blown rebuild — which may not be a bad idea — then Nacua should stay and get the contract he deserves. Even if the Rams do rebuild, who is Simpson supposed to be developing as a quarterback with?

Fowler says Nacua's career with the Rams is probably over. I say that's probably a shortsighted overreaction.

#2828. Nicolas Cage on his John Madden misfire: "I'm not Frank Caliendo"

This whole thing is antithetical to my identity.

That’s the one line that resonates most strongly in the new Madden movie. Because it’s exactly what John Madden would say if he saw it.

It’s bad. It’s very bad. Anyone who says it’s good has no taste and/or an agenda that involves the strategic application of lips to asses.

The biggest problem is Nicolas Cage as John Madden. Anyone who vividly remembers the unique charisma of John Madden knows instantly that nothing about Cage’s portrayal reflects the true nature, spirit, and demeanor of one of the most important and impactful figures in the entire history of the sport of football.

Cage, who seems to realize that his portrayal missed not only the bull’s-eye but also the entire wall on which the dart board was mounted, has defended the outcome by peering down his nose at the sports world.

“He was not on my radar,” Cage said of Madden, via Kirsten Chuba of the Hollywood Reporter. “I was growing up watching black-and-white Orson Welles movies and Fellini movies and Bruce Lee. I wasn’t interested in team sports whatsoever.”

“I’m someone that likes to stay out of his comfort zone and take a risk, I said yes, because that would be a transformation,” Cage explained regarding the decision to attempt to play the towering, iconic figure. “It would be something where I might learn a few things, taking on this character who is really nothing like me.”

The audience has learned that Cage’s interpretation is nothing like Madden.

“That’s what acting’s about,” Cage said. “I’m not an impressionist, I’m not Frank Caliendo. I lean more towards being a surrealist, meaning I like to get a concept of a personality and then dig deep and see what I can locate emotionally with my imagination and my psyche and filter it through the cadence and the appearance, within reason, of John Madden. I’m trying to give you an evocation, more or less, or an interpretation.”

The problem was it wasn’t even “within reason.” It was without reason. And the entire film was beyond unreasonable.

And I like Nicolas Cage. He was brilliant in Moonstruck. He won an Oscar for Leaving Las Vegas. And The Family Man remains a highly underrated holiday film.

Still, to quote another holiday film, “They can’t all be winners.” Cage’s role in Madden as John Madden is not.

I only met John Madden once. I watched him on TV for decades. I’ve heard plenty of stories about him from people who worked with him at NBC. And I’m confident that he would be livid about this film.

“That’s not me,” he’d say. “Not even close.”

Or, perhaps, “This whole thing is antithetical to my identity.”

#2827. Chiefs Fans Slam $3 Billion Stadium Design as Clark Hunt Considers Controversial New Fee

Kansas City Chiefs fans aren't happy with the team's plans for a new $3 billion stadium in Kansas. Many have criticized the dome design, while others are concerned they could soon have to pay more for season tickets.

The Chiefs plan to leave Arrowhead Stadium and move into the new 70,000-seat venue in 2031. However, after seeing images of the proposed stadium, some furious fans questioned why the team is replacing Arrowhead's open-air setting with a dome.

Adding to their frustration, Chiefs chairman Clark Hunt confirmed the team is considering personal seat licenses (PSLs), which would require season ticket holders to pay an additional fee just to purchase their seats.

The planned stadium has already drawn criticism from fans who believe the design looks too similar to other modern NFL venues.

Much of the frustration centers on the decision to build a dome rather than another outdoor stadium.

"Sweet… looks like every other stadium built in the last ten years. I'm sure a sellout stadium will be so much better than Arrowhead," one fan wrote on social media.

Another supporter commented, "Not a single soul likes this boring, recycled dome stadium."

Others questioned whether the new venue would offer the same experience as Arrowhead, which has been the Chiefs' home since 1972.

"We do not care. Chiefs fans do not want a dome!" one X user posted.

Another added, "Just like every other ugly domed stadium. No one is coming to 'experience' this as they do at Arrowhead. Generic trash with zero tradition or history."

Some fans also expressed frustration about not having a say in the stadium plans.

"Literally nobody asked for this. The people who bought tickets for 50 years and paid for this stadium had no say in this. 90% of us hate it," one supporter wrote.

The Chiefs have not announced changes to the proposed design in response to the criticism.

Beyond the stadium's appearance, fans are questioning how much it will cost to attend games at the new facility.

Hunt confirmed that the Chiefs are exploring personal seat licenses, which would require fans to purchase a license for their seats separately from their season tickets.

The team's agreement with Kansas allows the organization to implement the fees.

Several NFL teams, including the Buffalo Bills, Tennessee Titans and Las Vegas Raiders, have used similar arrangements.

However, some Chiefs supporters are unhappy about the possibility.

"Buffalo did it. Tennessee's done it. Vegas has done it. I mean, it's kind of the new thing," Chiefs fan David Whitaker said. "It's a scam."

Whitaker explained that his son currently holds season tickets and would likely continue attending games despite the additional expense.

"He's not happy about it, but I mean, I'm sure he'll pay. I mean, as most Chiefs fans will," Whitaker continued. "They love the team, want to support the team, but they don't like supporting the owners a lot of times, but they're going to do it."

Another fan, Larry Windham, questioned why season ticket holders should have to pay more.

"I think we already spent enough money on tickets and go into the game, the whole fan experience. I don't need an added fee that I have to come up with," Windham said.

The organization has not confirmed whether PSLs will be required when the new stadium opens.

Hunt said Thursday that he hopes longtime Arrowhead season ticket holders will be able to attend games at the new Kansas facility.

Chiefs president Mark Donovan previously discussed the possibility of seat licenses in December, saying polling results about fans' willingness to pay could be unexpected. He also argued that the licenses carry value for buyers.

The team has several years to make a final decision, with the stadium expected to be ready by August 2031.

Meanwhile, local businesses are considering how higher game-day costs could affect where fans choose to watch Chiefs games.

Crissi Tomlinson, a bartender at Tanner's Bar & Grill, pointed to the combined expenses of attending games in person.

"What you pay to just to park… to drinking, to eating, everything combined and all the money that you spend just to sit down and be able to watch the game, you know, it adds up," Tomlinson told Fox 4 Kansas City. "It's a lot of money, and you want to be able to enjoy it at the same time and have a fun atmosphere."

The bar plans to open at 5 p.m. Thursday for the Chiefs' game against the Buffalo Bills.

#2826. Davis, Dybantsa lead Wizards to second straight win

The Washington Wizards rode outstanding games from Anthony Davis and AJ Dybantsa to escape Chicago with a second straight victory.

For a second straight game, the win wasn't easy, pretty, or satisfying. But it was a win. Davis dominated inside against a Bulls roster lacking a serious NBA big man. He finished with 36 points and 11 rebounds.

For my money, the most heartening thing from last night's contest was the performance of Dybantsa, who notched 20 points, 10 rebounds, and 6 assists. Reminder: he's still just 19 years old. His first step, vertical burst, and power seem surprising even in the ultra-athletic NBA — even to his ultra-athletic NBA competitors.

It's a good thing Davis and Dybantsa were great because the rest of the team didn't help much. Trae Young was okay — 16 points, 5 assists, 3 steals, and just 1 turnover. He shot 4-8 from three-point range…and 0-5 from two.

Bilal Coulibaly contributed next to nothing on offense but harassed Chicago's perimeter players on the defensive end and came up with two steals and two blocks. One of those blocks was great — with just over three minutes to go in the fourth quarter, Bulls wing Norman Powell drove. Coulibaly moved his feet, stayed with Powell step for step, stayed between Powell and the basket, and then maintained verticality when Powell pulled up. Powell ended up shooting the ball into Coulibaly's raised (and vertical) hand.

Once again, the Wizards went with a short postseason-like rotation. Head coach Brian Keefe used just eight players for more than 10 minutes, and Deandre Ayton got just 11 minutes total. Will Riley, Bub Carrington, and Tre Johnson made cameo appeareances — 6, 6, and 4 minutes respectively.

To me, it seems that Keefe trusts only a handful of players — Young, Davis, Dybantsa, and Kyshawn George. He wants to trust Alex Sarr, and Bilal Coulibaly. He's using other guys, like Khris Middleton, Ayton, Tre Johnson, Will Riley and Bub Carrington because he has to play someone.

The Bulls pregame intro video is great. It depicts charging bulls stampeding into the stadium. At one point, the herd turns towards a bus with a Wizards logo on it. A couple "players" descending the bus steps, spot the herd and flee in a panic. It amused me.

One other shoutout to the Bulls game operations crew — thank you for having a real halftime act. Last night, it was Christian and Scooby, which is an act that has not gotten old yet.

The Wizards had a terrible first possession of the game. They ran a bunch of actions to end up with George attempting a fading, drifting, contested three from the corner. Their offensive effectiveness didn't get much better. They managed an offensive rating (points scored per 100 possessions) of 101. League average this season is 114.4.

They won despite a poor offensive game because Chicago's offensive performance was somehow even worse.

The negatives keep piling up for George. Last night, he shot 5-17 from the floor and 1-8 from three-point range, and added three turnovers and five fouls. At least two of the fouls were of the dumb and pointless variety. Just hacking or grabbing an opponent for no discernible reason. Another was an offensive foul (shoving Isaac Okoro out of his way with a forearm) that might be the easiest call the refs make this season.

A play midway through the second quarter reminded me how good NBA players are. Zach Collins, a backup big man on one of the NBA's worst teams drove to the basket and spun into a lefty hook over Davis. It was an impressive display of skill, athleticism, and coordination from an NBA afterthought.

Much as I enjoy watching Dybantsa play, he can get sped up by strong defensive pressure. Several possessions per game have gotten frantic and messy. I'm looking forward to seeing those possessions cleaned up as he gains experience.

Around 8:24 in the fourth quarter, Dybantsa swooped in for an eye-popping reverse dunk in transition.

Maybe 20 seconds earlier, Coulibaly picked Powell's dribble and took the ball the other way for a breakaway dunk.

The Wizards were down eight at the half, and then blasted the Bulls, 23-9, in the third quarter and nursed the leae the rest of the ways.

4:32 — AD postup into a stepback — miss — bad shot

3:20 — impressive defense by BC — moves feet, good position, goes vertical and Powell shoots ball into BC's hand for a block

Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made).

eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot)

TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions)

FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts)

can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn't much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results.

POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game.

ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist.

USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median last season was 17.7%.

ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers.

+PTS = "Plus Points" is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0.

Players are sorted by total production in the game.

#2824. Bears have a chance to prove a key prediction wrong in Week 11 vs. Saints

With newly acquired defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons in the fold, the Chicago Bears' defensive outlook and philosophy have undergone a major shift for the better.

That's not just from an individual perspective, though Simmons has been great in that regard, posting three tackles for loss, two sacks, and two passes defended in his two weeks with the Bears. The unit as a whole has benefited from the increased double teams the All-Pro tackle has faced, allowing just 4.5 yards per play when he's been on the field and ranking in the top 10 in EPA/play and success rate allowed since Simmons got here.

But there's one aspect in which, while improved, the Bears have remained somewhat middling at: defending the run. That's why NFL.com's Brooke Cersosimo forecasts New Orleans Saints running back Travis Etienne might be a problem for Chicago on Sunday.

"Etienne returned to action last week after missing five games with a hamstring injury and looked rusty — to say the least — rushing for 14 yards on eight carries. He turns things around in dramatic fashion against the Bears on Sunday with his first 100-yard rushing performance and touchdown of the season," Cersosimo wrote for her bold prediction for this week in NFL action.

When healthy, Etienne is one of the better dual-threat backs in the league. But nothing about his performance in his first season with the Saints suggests he's either of those things (142 rushing yards on 38 carries). In fact, no one in New Orleans running backs room has done much worth writing home about: through nine games, quarterback Tyler Shough leads the team with 187 rushing yards. That's ugly.

The Saints have a true running-by-committee squad, ravaged by a combination of injuries and ineffectiveness. So it's unlikely any of them gets enough action on their own to approach 100 yards rushing unless one of them gets hot. From what we've seen, there's nothing to suggest that'll happen. Plus, if the Bears come out hot on offense and put Shough and the Saints in catch-up mode, you can forget about Etienne as a rushing threat. That, no doubt, is part of what the Bears hope to do.

But it's also important to note just how big a deal this Simmons acquisition has been for Chicago.

Because yes, the Bears defense has been pretty uninspiring against the run for the past couple of years, and a player with Etienne's skill set could definitely have given them trouble in a game like this before Simmons arrived.

These days, though, the Bears have the look of a squad bent on changing that reputation (as long as Simmons stays healthy and on the field himself). The presence of an elite defensive tackle has everyone playing better, especially speedy linebacker Devin Bush.

Again, there's nothing wrong with a bold prediction or two. But let's stash an Etienne 100-yard game in the "highly unlikely" category.

#2822. AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."

Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.

The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."

CNBC did not independently verify this information.

Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."

The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.

"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

#2820. The Celtics, in all of their early-season glory, haven’t passed Brad Stevens’ test yet

We're about a fifth of the way through the 2026-27 Boston Celtics season.

So far, mostly so good. The Celtics are 11-4, which has them slotted second in the East behind the Philadelphia 76ers — whom they beat in comfortable fashion last week at Xfinity Mobile Arena, 123-101.

For you analytics heads out there, Boston ranks sixth in offensive rating, second in defensive rating, and second in net rating.

Paul George, whom the Cs bet on when they traded Jaylen Brown for him (and some nice picks) couldn't be playing much better. If you need any insight into how the PG-13 Experience has been, look no further than the fanbase collectively referring to him as "Paul God."

The other offseason addition hasn't panned out as well, but we won't jump on the pile here.

Through this first month, the only real nitpick about this team is the schedule that they've had. Multiple games against the putrid Milwaukee Bucks and Chicago Bulls, plus a handful against other struggling squads like the Charlotte Hornets, Dallas Mavericks, Toronto Raptors, and Brooklyn Nets make the 11-4 record feel a bit inflated.

Don't take my word for it; here's what Brad Stevens had to say about last season's 56-win team in his end-of-season press conference.

"We have to play well in the regular season to get to where we want to go," he told reporters back in May. "We don't want to undersell the regular season. That said, as I look at us honestly, I look at how we played against the best teams is relevant and should be taken into account as we look at our team moving forward."

Boston's record against the top three teams in each conference was 3-11. Of course, their first-round loss to the 76ers only amplified that issue. The Sixers weren't a "top team" but at full-strength (which they miraculously were in Games 4-7), they're not your typical Play-In team.

Anyway, there was a clear correlation in all the losses vs. that in the wins. Boston shot just 27.4% from three in the losses. In victories, that number jumped up to 41.7%.

This season, they haven't quite shown us that it'll be a different story just yet. The Cs have had five games against teams above .500 and have won just two. Their three losses came agains the Detroit Pistons, Houston Rockets, and Denver Nuggets.

The two wins have featured elite shooting performances from the perimeter. Boston sank 16-40 in their home opener against the New York Knicks, and then lit the Sixers up with a 22-49 performance in Philly.

Somehow, they lost the opener against Detroit despite a strong shooting day, but the other two losses have gone exactly how you'd guess.

I know how this all sounds, too. Like yeah, of course they're going to shoot better in wins than losses — you could probably pull up the splits for every team in the league and they'd look the same.

With the Celtics, though, it's #DifferentHere. A team that's relied so heavily on winning the mathematical margins over the past four seasons has seen shooting variance end three of them in disappointing fashion. The 2024 team was special, but also managed to win playoff games when they went cold — even they dropped a few headscratchers thanks to variance.

Does this all mean that this season's team sucks?

Probably not. But it's disappointing that they've come up short a few times in their limited amount of "prove it" games. Their lost to Houston did come on the second night of a back-to-back where Paul God was resting. So, there's some grace to be given there.

One optimistic takeaway so far has been the elite defense. Boston's 106.0 defensive rating has been built on sharp rotations, disruptive defensive playmaking, and a strong paint presence from Neemias Queta. All three of those things will remain under their control regardless of whether or not the shots are going in on a given night.

The Celtics have held opponents to under 110 points in 11 of their 15 games thus far. By doing so, they're at least giving themselves a chance to get across the finish line when the threes don't fall. We might be watching them develop their backup plan in real time.

It's going to be a while before another "test" game. Their NBA Cup group stage finale against the Atlanta Hawks will be a minor test before they head to San Antonio to take on the Spurs next Sunday. A win against Wemby and the reigning West champs would go along way in battling the "schedule merchants" narratives.

#2819. Ravens’ 2026 season has come to a crashing halt

It took just one play. As optimistically as it began, the 2026 Ravens season is all but finished. On the first day of November, on his first snap back from a high-ankle sprain, Lamar Jackson injured his right thumb when his throwing hand struck the wrist of Bills pass rusher Greg Rousseau. Jackson knew something was wrong immediately, sprinting straight to the sideline and then to the locker room.

The two-time MVP has since had surgery on his thumb with a late-season return technically in play – if it even matters.

At this point, Jackson is the Baltimore Ravens, and his contract reflects that. Many want to bash the supporting cast, the coaches and the front office, but it just isn't realistic for a team paying a star quarterback that much to also have stars at every other position. What did the Chiefs look like without Patrick Mahomes last year? What did the Bengals look like without Joe Burrow? What would the Bills look like without Josh Allen?

On top of losing Jackson, the Ravens have suffered a rash of injuries elsewhere, primarily on the offensive line. A position group that typically thrives on continuity is operating with a new offensive coordinator, a new offensive line coach, and a rotating door of new starters. This year, the unit has had five different centers and four different right guards. Has the offensive line been good enough? No. But we never got to see the vision. Heck, we never even got to see Jackson and Zay Flowers play a full game together.

The full extent of the Ravens' woes came to a head five days after the Jacksonville Jaguars. With undrafted rookie quarterback Joe Fagnano making his first start, the Ravens were once again trounced at home, this time in a downpour. We all expected the offense to struggle, and predictably, it did. But once again, the defense let the dam break. Is that partly a product of the offense's struggles? Probably. Still, it looked more like a group of unmotivated, aging players struggling to adjust to a new defensive system. Marlon Humphrey and Malaki Starks were both burned for big plays, and the middle of the field — an area that has plagued this defense for years — was wide open all night for Trevor Lawrence.

And yet, Monday night's loss to the Chargers might have been worse. Jacoby Brissett performed admirable in his Ravens debut, but an anemic running game and a defense that once again could not tackle gifted a winless team their first victory.

Unfortunately, the near future doesn't look much brighter, largely because of some questionable decisions by the front office. The Ravens' so-called "star" veterans by salary have underperformed this year. Marlon Humphrey, Roquan Smith, Ronnie Stanley, Mark Andrews and John Simpson make up more than 25% of the Ravens' salary cap. That's not a winning formula.

It's easy to engage in revisionist history on contracts. Humphrey signed his extension in 2020 and Smith signed his in early 2023. Since then, both have followed the natural arc of an NFL second contract: some very good years, and now the back end of their careers. Humphrey was an All-Pro in 2024, and Smith was an All-Pro in 2022 and 2023. Their decline isn't surprising. What's surprising is that the Ravens have forgotten one of Ozzie Newsome's favorite phrases: 'better to move on from a player a year too early rather than a year too late.' It might be two years late for Humphrey now. Smith's decision point should be this offseason. His oversized contract is arguably worse. Fred Warner is probably the only middle linebacker in the NFL worth that kind of money. Humphrey has virtually seen himself out the door in the last week; if the Ravens are committed to change, Smith should be gone this offseason, too.

Now let's talk about Mark Andrews. In my opinion, re-signing him was the worst contract DeCosta has ever handed out. Andrews has been terrible. So bad that he's actively hurting the team. From 2019 to 2025, the Ravens consistently had one of the best tight end rooms in the league. Now it's one of the worst. Meanwhile, as many of us suspected he would, Isaiah Likely is looking like one of the best tight ends in football. For his entire tenure in Baltimore, we assumed he'd be Andrews' successor.

That said, I don't think it's fair to claim the Ravens have simply punted on the trenches. On defense, Trey Hendrickson, Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones all got paid. On the offensive line, the Ravens re-signed Ronnie Stanley, traded picks for center Cam Jurgens, spent their 2026 first-round pick on a guard and drafted Roger Rosengarten in the second round. The problem is that those players aren't playing up to their price. Stanley and Rosengarten are both playing like average tackles. On the interior, Jurgens has been fine, but he hasn't looked like he is worth a second-round pick. John Simpson hasn't been much better than what the Ravens had at guard last year, though he's dealt with a groin injury for most of the season.

The Ravens trust their development process to a fault. Sometimes it's paid off, but there have been far too many instances where it hasn't, especially on the offensive line. Emery Jones Jr., Andrew Vorhees and Daniel Faalele have been abject developmental failures.

Some of it is just bad luck. Ronnie Stanley was one of the best tackles in the NFL before his gruesome ankle injury. Since then, he's played just well enough to earn another contract. But that's the issue: the Ravens have been fine with "just good enough." Rather than proactively building a dominant offensive line, they've settled for adequate. Look at the elite teams in the NFL right now. The Bills, 49ers, Lions, Bears, Broncos and even the Steelers all have top offensive lines. Obviously, if it were that easy, every team would do it. But when you have a superstar quarterback, protecting him is paramount.

In a way, the 2024 season did them in. Despite two below-average guards, the Ravens put together a record-setting offense, so naturally, DeCosta thought it prudent to run it back. Let's face it: when Jackson is healthy, the Ravens have typically had great offenses regardless of who's blocking for him. Even this year, the Ravens ranked second in EPA per play with Jackson and this current group.The downside is that when Jackson is injured or hobbled, the team falls apart because the line can't impose its will on opponents.

If the Ravens are serious about building a championship team, they need to pour as many resources as possible into the trenches. Teams don't fear playing the Ravens anymore because they've become largely a finesse team, with undersized corners, offensive linemen, linebackers and receivers. As a result, they can't salt away games like they used to. In the second half, when opponents know the run is coming, the Ravens get shut down. Their status as one of the league's worst short-yardage teams reflects that.In the early stages of the Lamar Jackson era, the major question was whether the Ravens could play from behind. They were that good at putting opponents away. Now it's the opposite.

DeCosta also has a habit of overcorrecting for past problems. The Ravens struggled to draft and develop receivers, so he spent multiple first-round picks trying to find one instead of trading for an established star, the way the team did with Anquan Boldin. The Ravens went through a few years where they couldn't keep cornerbacks healthy, so he overcorrected again, spending pick after pick on corners to make sure it wouldn't happen again. The better approach: trade for stars at the positions you've historically failed to develop.

DeCosta also has a habit of being too loyal to his players. In one of his first press conferences as general manager, he talked about wanting to stop letting players walk out the door. The result has been long contracts that haven't lived up to their value. Compare that with Eagles GM Howie Roseman, who's an expert at trading players at peak value before they decline. A.J. Brown, whom the Eagles acquired for a first-round pick, was dealt to New England for a first-rounder. Roseman did the same with Jordan Davis and even Cam Jurgens, whom the Ravens probably overpaid for. DeCosta has done the opposite. Perhaps seeing the roster through purple-tinted glasses, he has consistently held on to players too long. Fittingly, the best move of his career may have been trading away Hollywood Brown for an extra first-round pick, which he used to select Tyler Linderbaum.

The Ravens desperately need a reload, along with more juice and playmaking. Aside from Jackson, their only true playmakers are Zay Flowers and Kyle Hamilton. Even Derrick Henry, as great as he's been, needs good blocking to get going. He isn't great at making defenders miss at the line of scrimmage or creating something out of nothing. Obviously, once he gets past the first level, he's devastating. But he's 32,and I'd love to see the Ravens pair Jackson with a different style of running back — one with three-down ability who can create yardage on his own. I'm not saying they should show Henry the door, but they should start building a contingency plan.

The rest of this season will be about the development of players like Mike Green, Malaki Starks, Ja'Kobi Lane, T.J. Tampa, Zion Young and Trenton Simpson. All have shown flashes, and if a few of them ascend to stardom, the Ravens' future will look much brighter.

The defense also has to improve as a whole. There have been stretches where it's looked good, but too often we see the same issues that have plagued it for the last three years: an inconsistent pass rush, an inability to get off the field on third down and receivers getting too much separation. DeCosta has poured resources into the secondary with all four starters being first-round picks. Unfortunately, the result has been a massive letdown. Humphrey has been a liability for two years, but his running mate, Nate Wiggins, has been far from a star, with a 61.6 grade from Pro Football Focus that currently ranks 53rd out of 110 corners (min. 150 snaps). Malaki Starks, the 2025 first-rounder, has also been inconsistent. Coming out of college, Starks was billed as a versatile chess piece, but he's looked bad in coverage. Ironically, he looks far more comfortable as a box safety, the role Kyle Hamilton typically occupies.

DeCosta and the Ravens have frequently preached that they want a "positionless" defense built on players who can line up all over the field. Unfortunately, very few NFL players are good enough to do that. Hamilton is obviously one of them, but it's becoming clear that Starks isn't, and he should be put in a role that maximizes his skill set.

The 2026 season may be over, and the next few years look bleak right now, but there are some positives as the Ravens move into their next era. First, many of these underperforming veterans will be gone next year, giving the Ravens a chance to get younger. They also have a solid nucleus of players in their prime: Jackson, Ioane, Hamilton, Flowers, Hendrickson and Madubuike. However, there will be questions about some of the other established veterans. Will Ronnie Stanley be in Baltimore next year? What about Derrick Henry?

Lastly, there's the issue of Lamar Jackson. When healthy, Jackson is arguably the best player in the NFL. The problem is that, whether because of shaky protection or otherwise, he simply hasn't been on the field as much as the Ravens need him. This team is built around him. He is the Baltimore Ravens, and the team goes as he goes. Jackson carries a massive cap hit next year, and his no-trade clause gives him all the leverage in negotiations. Heading into next year, DeCosta will probably have to hand him a blank check. We've seen this dynamic play out before: in 2023, Jackson waited until Jalen Hurts signed his extension before agreeing to his own market-setting deal in Baltimore. Owner Steve Bisciotti was adamant at the start of this season that he wants Jackson to be the highest-paid player in the NFL. Unless Jackson doesn't want to be in Baltimore, which would contradict nearly every report about his re-energized demeanor this year, a deal will get done.

It's a disappointing way for this season to go. In the one game this team was truly healthy, it steamrolled the Colts in Week 1. Since then, it's been a revolving door of quarterbacks, receivers and offensive linemen. People will point fingers, and there will be constant speculation about Lamar Jackson's future in Baltimore. Ultimately, though, I view this as a season that had potential but never came together. Hopefully, Eric DeCosta can quickly reload the roster, shed some dead weight and put the Ravens back in contention by the start of 2027.

#2818. Tyler Herro scores career-high 50 points but his final 3 doesn't beat the buzzer and the Bucks lose

PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Tyler Herro let his final shot of the game fly and — just as the Bucks guard had felt throughout his career-best game — thought it was good.

LeBron James assumed Herro would make the tying bucket, and force overtime.

"Just the way he was playing and the way his shot-making was tonight, I was like, 'It's going in,'" James said.

The Sixers star had one more thought in the moment as the final seconds ticked off the clock.

"And hopefully he didn't get it off in time," James said.

Herro's shot from the right wing did indeed go in to temporarily stun the Philadelphia crowd. He just couldn't beat the buzzer and instead finished with his first career 50-point game — in another Bucks loss.

"Great execution," Bucks coach Taylor Jenkins said. "Wish we had a little bit more time."

Officials huddled around the monitors to confirm the call. The verdict was in: "The field goal was released after ...," as the crowd of 21,043 erupted and drowned out the rest of the announcement.

Herro had the NBA's sixth 50-point game of the season, hitting seven 3-pointers with 11 rebounds and making all 13 free throws, just not enough to lift the Bucks as the 76ers held on for a 132-129 win on Saturday.

Milwaukee lost its 13th in a row and 16th in 17 contests to start the season.

"I thought I beat the clock," Herro said. "But I did have a little like, it was close. But that's my go-to shot, fading right on that right wing. Coach knew it and drew up the play for me to do it. I just needed like point-five seconds, maybe less than that to get it off."

Herro made 15 of 23 shots overall from the floor. He scored 15 points in each of the first, third and fourth quarters against James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and a Sixers team that improved to 14-3.

"He was great. We didn't do as good a job as we should have done," Embiid said. "But sometimes, people get hot and have good nights, and he did a great job tonight."

Herro's previous best was 41 points against Houston on Dec. 15, 2022.

The 26-year-old Herro spent his first seven seasons with the Miami Heat before the summer trade that sent him to his hometown team. Herro, a Milwaukee-area native who graduated from nearby Whitnall High School in Greenfield, Wisconsin, has this final season remaining on his contract and could become an unrestricted free agent after the 2026-27 season if he doesn't get an extension.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar had 10 career 50-point games for the Bucks and Giannis Antetokounmpo — sent to Miami in the offseason in the deal that brought Herro on board — had nine. Michael Redd added two 50-pointers, and Herro joined Jrue Holiday, Brandon Jennings and Khris Middleton in the one-time 50-point scorers club.

Herro grew up rooting for the Bucks and was happy to join such an accomplished list of 50-point scorers.

"It's obviously great to be in that category with a lot of great Milwaukee Bucks," Herro said.

Herro joined the Bucks eager to bounce back from a 2025-26 season in which injuries limited him to only 33 games. Herro has averaged over 20 points each of the last five seasons, and he earned an All-Star selection in 2025.

He averaged 19.4 points entering the game but combined for just 13 points in two losses this week to Atlanta and Miami.

"I had the ball in my hands a little bit more than I've had, like, the last couple of weeks or so, the last week or so," Herro said. "The more I have the ball in my hands, the more I'm going to continue to make the right play. Coach has been stressing that for the last month. Continue to make the right play, points will come."

#2817. Philadelphia mayor wants the Eagles to play in a dome

The Eagles will become an indoor team if the mayor of Philadelphia gets her way.

“I want a dome,” Mayor Charelle L. Parker said on 93.3 WMMR, via the Philadelphia Inquirer. “Don’t you tell. This is a secret between us. I just saw a rendering of this beautiful dome that they’re talking about for the Bears.”

Moving into a dome would change the character of late-season and playoff games in Philadelphia, which are often affected by snow, wind and cold. Plenty of fans won’t like it. But politicians and NFL owners often prefer stadiums with roofs because they bring in lucrative events, indoor sports, concerts, conventions and trade shows.

The Eagles told season ticket holders last year that they are looking at either renovations to Lincoln Financial Field or a new stadium. Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie has committed only to staying in “the region,” not in the city of Philadelphia, but both Parker and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro have said they want the Eagles to remain in the city.

The Eagles’ lease at Lincoln Financial Field runs through the 2032 season.

#2816. From 1-5 to above .500, the Suns are doing something right

The Phoenix Suns are a game above .500. When this team started the season 1-5, I wasn't entirely convinced I'd have the opportunity to type those words anytime soon. Yet here we are, thanks to some improved chemistry, particularly among the starting unit, and a favorable stretch of the schedule.

How much of this resurgence can be attributed to genuine improvement versus the quality of competition? Only time will tell. We spend so much time dissecting how games are won or lost that we occasionally lose sight of a rather important detail. A win is a win. And in the NBA, every single one of them matters.

Yes, the Suns defeated the Utah Jazz by 10 points on Friday night, despite allowing Utah to trim the deficit to four in the closing minutes. Naturally, some will point to that late surge as evidence that this wasn't a particularly impressive victory. The funny thing? Many of those same people will dismiss Wednesday's win over the Sacramento Kings because, well, that's what the Suns were supposed to do. Don't be that guy.

Phoenix put itself in a position to win on Friday night, although Utah certainly helped the cause by missing 13 free throws. The result? A third consecutive road victory and a team that suddenly finds itself on the right side of .500.

Winning in the NBA is hard. I don't care who you're playing, how many injuries the opposing team is dealing with, or how ugly the basketball might look at times. Every team in this league has talented players capable of making your life miserable on any given night. Funny how that works, too. When an undermanned opponent beats the Suns, we're quick to praise their resilience and talk about how there's still some fight in that dog. But when Phoenix beats an undermanned opponent, suddenly the victory comes with an asterisk in the court of public opinion.

The win over Utah wasn't necessarily pretty. Some stretches made you uncomfortable, moments that invited frustration, and a fourth quarter that probably didn't need to be as interesting as it became. But it was effective. It added another victory to the win column, extended the momentum of a successful road trip, and gave the Suns something positive to carry into Monday's matchup against the New Orleans Pelicans.

It certainly beats the alternative. Never forget that alternative, either. Because if the Suns had blown that lead and lost to Utah, we'd be spending the next 48 hours dissecting every possession, questioning every rotation decision, and wondering whether this team had learned a damn thing from its early struggles.

Instead? Good win. Hop on the plane. On to the next city.

#2814. Alabama football TE Josh Ford donned helmet with crutches for a reason

Alabama football TE Josh Ford has a reputation for being a hitter, and a season-ending knee injury didn't prevent him from living up to it.

Prior to the Crimson Tide's 47-0 win over Chattanooga on Saturday, Nov. 21, Ford, despite being on crutches, wore a football helmet on the sideline. It's an odd look for any player who knows he won't be playing, but for the transfer from Oklahoma State, his helmet had a purpose.

"He got his helmet on and was head-butting people with a messed up knee," said fellow tight end Kaleb Edwards. "That's the kind of guy he is; he's going to hyped up no matter what."

Ford was known to do just that before his injury, doing what he could to lift intensity among his teammates. Since getting hurt in the fourth quarter of UA's road win at LSU, however, helping from the sideline is all the impact Ford can make for the balance of the season.

Ford made only five receptions for 41 yards and two touchdowns for the season, but was highly valued as a blocker who could handle both linemen and linebackers alike. Edwards has been among multiple players to see more action in Ford's absence, and caught three passes for a team-high 63 yards against the Mocs.

Alabama plays host to archrival Auburn next Saturday.

#2813. Daiyan Henley being out with a knee injury changes nothing about the failed trade to Broncos

The failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley returned to the front burner on Friday, with the news that Henley will miss Sunday’s game against the Jets due to a knee injury.

It was a knee condition that prompted the Broncos to pull the plug on the deal — after trying to renegotiate the terms after the trade deadline.

From Mike Klis of 9News, who covers the Broncos: “Chargers ILB Daiyan Henley missed entire week of practices with knee injury and has been ruled out for game vs Jets. This validates concerns raised by Broncos medical team and GM George Paton. And proves Chargers were not on the up and up.”

Does it really prove that the Chargers weren’t “on the up and up”? The issue is that the Denver physical flagged a knee problem. In lieu of finding that the physical had been failed and that the trade won’t happen, the Broncos were willing to give Henley a passing grade, if the compensation was changed.

Henley has played every game this season. He played on Monday night against the Ravens. As far as anyone knows, he injured the knee during that game.

As far as anyone knows, the currently injured knee isn’t the same knee that created the concern during the Denver physical.

It’s all just noise at this point. The core problem is the ability of a team — after the trade deadline has passed — to renegotiate the terms of a trade. And the related issue is the ability of a team to give a conditional grade on the pass-fail question of a physical that is tied to the specific compensation.

A player either passes the physical, or he fails it. The process shouldn’t include an epilogue premised on the outcome of the physical being “maybe.” Especially after the time for negotiating trades has ended.
