#2812. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2811. NBA: Top 5 Wolves Games I’ve Attended

Over the years, I've been very blessed to attend a litany of exciting Timberwolves games, many in the playoffs. Now being a Gen-Z'er, these all came in the Anthony Edwards era. I wish I could've seen Kevin Garnett live, but unfortunately his prime came before my time as a serious basketball watcher.

Here are my top five games that I've attended and my point-of-view, in reverse order.

The entire 2023-24 season was an absolute whirlwind and the lead up to this game was no different. I was entirely confident the Wolves were going to blitz the Dallas Mavericks as we'd advance to the NBA Finals, but alas that was not the case. I cannot begin the immense joy I felt walking into Target Center that night, with pregame drinks at Cowboy Jack's across the street, of course. I hit the team store to get some Conference Finals merch, took some pictures of the TNT crew (including Draymond Green, ew), and even got to my seat damn near in the rafters.

It was pure bliss, only to get my heart ripped out two and a half hours later. Even though Minnesota lost, it was still a close game with high stakes and as just a fan of the sport, I was enthralled. Had the Wolves won this game it would've been higher, but it lands on my list at number five.

The story of my time at this game begins at Blue Door Pub on Como Avenue in Minneapolis. Only living a couple blocks away, I had never been and my time there was spent nervously eating a Juicy Lucy and worrying about the game. If you may remember, Phoenix was widely thought of as the prohibitive favorite. Guys like Devin Booker and Kevin Durant terrified me, as to that point the Timberwolves hadn't won a playoff series since 2004.

The Wolves absolutely took over. Anthony Edwards was hitting step-back threes over Durant while jawing at him. Naz Reid was hitting "jelly" reverse layups on the fastbreak. I almost couldn't believe it. Watching your team win like that, especially live…there's nothing like it. Because I attended this game and it went well, a tradition was sparked with my roommates and I: Since we had watched the game apart, I now had to watch the games alone and away from them to preserve those good vibes. I can't say it didn't work, either, as I watched games two, three, and four from my room as Minnesota swept Phoenix.

Man, this was fun. For the first time in my basketball watching life, a Timberwolves team enjoyed success in a playoff setting. Riding some irrational confidence, I didn't think that there was any way that a LA Clippers team led by Paul George (still called "Pandemic P" at the time) was going to stop the Wolves from setting a date with the Memphis Grizzlies in the first round.

George had a great game, hitting big shot after big shot. Things weren't exactly going great on the Timberwolves side of things because if you remember, Karl-Anthony Towns was in major foul trouble for most of the game. Then D'Angelo Russell started making shots. Anthony Edwards made a couple big plays. Before I knew it, I was watching Patrick Beverly throw the ball up in the air as the buzzer sounds and jump up onto the scorer's table like the Wolves had just won the NBA Finals.

To all the NBA fans who clown us Wolves fans for that reaction and our appreciation of it: take a hike. You never had to experience the suck that was a Luke Ridnour-Alexey Shved backcourt. As far as meaningful games I've attended, this may take the top spot. However, this list is the best games, so it lands at number three. I say meaningful because I attended this game with just my dad. He is the one who raised me to be a basketball fan and taught me most of what I know about the game, and to share the moment of our favorite team advancing for the first time since I was two years old with him was absolutely special. I'll never forget it.

The most recent game on my list slides in at number two. Anthony Edwards was out. Donte DiVincenzo had torn his Achille's. Then just hours before the game, it was announced that Ayo Dosunmu was going to be out. I was convinced that Jaden McDaniels and Julius Randle were not going to be enough to finish the Nuggets with most of their cast of characters. Denver would be able to focus their efforts on Jaden, who earlier in the series had dropped the "They're all bad defenders" line.

In the building, it felt like most Timberwolves fans felt the same. Minnesota blitzed Denver early as Julius made some tough buckets flanked by TJ Shannon being a menace in transition. Then as the game went on and the Wolves remained neck and neck with the Nuggets, even earning a lead, belief started to creep in. Denver wasn't going away though. I really thought they were going to pull some voodoo magic out of Jokić's horse racing hat and push this series to a seventh game. I was pushed further down this line of thinking when Jokić and Jaylen Clark got into a scuffle, resulting in two Minnesota technical fouls while Denver only received one.

Then, Jaden McDaniels showed everyone the player he truly is.

A couple made threes, a couple mir-range shots, and plenty of drives to the rim where he proved himself right: the Nuggets were all bad defenders. 32 points and 10 rebounds for Jaden that night, and a massive statement to the rest of the league that even though the Wolves were down their best three guards, their pack was not left defenseless.

Yes, the best game I have ever attended in person is a 45-point blowout victory.

Everyone remembers this series, but they remember it for the epic Game 7 comeback. What gets lost in the shuffle is that the Timberwolves blitzed Denver to the tune of a 2-0 series lead before the Nuggets came back with a Balboa-level haymaker to take a series lead of 3-2. This Game 6 was an elimination game for Minnesota, and it didn't start very well. The Nuggets jumped out to a 9-2 lead after just three minutes of play.

What followed that opening stanza of that game can only be described as a waxing.

Blink and you would've missed a 24-2 Timberwolves run. The Nuggets made a couple runs, sure, but it was never all that close again. Hell, even Jordan McLaughlin and Luka Garza got minutes on the floor in a Game 6 in the playoffs. That's how lopsided this victory was. Euphoria is the only feeling I can describe from the crowd at Target Center that night. Every Wolves fan wearing the "I <3 Wolves" t-shirt left happy that night. The team we absolutely hate had a chance to knock us off our Cinderella ride early, on our floor even. Saying "Hell No" and forcing a Game 7 was the only thing we could do, and we did it in crushing fashion.

#2807. Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.

Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2803. Division games a true barometer of Raiders progress, or lack of it

Divisional games just hit different in the NFL.

Featuring the twice-a-year meetings which lead to some heated rematches, the weight division games carry are much heavier than the standard affair of matchups league schedule makers put forth amongst the 32 teams. When the AFC and NFC teams in the East, North, South, and West tango, the playoff stakes are higher (I'll explain this more below) alongside familiarity creating either nail-biter meetings lopsided beatdowns.

It'll be intriguing to see which way the Las Vegas Raiders road trip to the Denver Broncos this Sunday plays out. Will it be an AFC West slugfest that's close? Or will the bucking Broncos trample the visiting Raiders?

With four of the final seven games on Las Vegas' slate being AFC West tilts — at Denver this Sunday; hosting the Los Angeles Chargers (Week 14, Dec. 13); hosting the Broncos (Week 15, Dec. 20); and at the Kansas City Chiefs (Week 18, Jan. 10) — we're going to see how much progress Klint Kubiak's Raiders have made — or the lack of it.

Kubiak, the heralded offensive mind who the Silver & Black tabbed as its 27th head coach in franchise history, has a storied history with Denver as he grew up around the team thanks to his father Gary, who spent decades as a Broncos player, offensive coordinator, head coach, and senior personnel advisory.

"Yeah, many memories. Looking forward to going back to the stadium and being a part of this game. Extremely excited for our team," the stoic younger Klint Kubiak said when asked about a memory that stands out as he heads back to Denver, this time, as a rookie head coach. "I think when I was blessed enough to get hired here to coach the Raiders, I thought about games in Denver and games in Kansas City and being a part of this division, so it's something that I've definitely thought about before. And now that we're in it, we're in the season. It's just next practice."

Kubiak is set to lead his 4-6 Raiders against Sean Peyton's 7-2 Broncos highlighting the different spectrums of success the two division foes are currently at. A win keeps Denver in-line with the 7-2 Chiefs and an all-important AFC West title and high seed in the postseason race. A victory by Las Vegas puts a nice shiner on Denver's division title hunt.

As Broncos wide receiver Courtland Sutton aptly mentioned above, the division games often lead to close, hard-fought one-score contests because teams know each other so well that tendencies are identified and counters properly installed. Even when one team is the cellar desperately trying to climb out, it can give a team atop the mountain with lofty goals in their eyes a difficult time gameday. This is a direct result of that deep familiarity and competitive drive amongst players and coaches.

As they say, familiarity breeds contempt and there's no love lost between the Raiders and Broncos — heck, the entire AFC West.

Las Vegas intends to be in the spot Denver is now — fighting for the division crown, a ticket to the postseason dance, and a legitimate chase for another Lombardi Trophy — and the future is now as the team traded trusty veteran Kirk Cousins and are now on the Fernando Mendoza era at quarterback. The rookie and No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft is well aware of what Week 11 presents for the Silver & Black.

"It's a great challenge. It's a rivalry game. If you can't get excited for a rivalry game, then there might be something wrong with you," Mendoza said. "So, I'm incredibly excited to take on the challenge. They're a great opponent. They have a great team. They have a great coach and a great quarterback. So, I'm looking forward to taking it on with my teammates."

Through the 10 games the Raiders have played this season, the team is 1-1 in AFC West play (beat the Chargers 26-14 in Week 2; lost to the Chiefs 30-27 in Week 4) and are 3-3 against AFC foes. The Broncos, on the other hand, are coming off their bye week and are 2-1 in division games played (lost the Chiefs 31-10 in Week 1; beat the Chargers 23-17 in Week 5, topped the Chiefs 28-24 in Week 8) and are 3-1 in AFC play through their nine games on the year.

Kubiak needs to get complementary football from his Raiders where his offense combines with Rob Leonard's defense, and Joe DeCamillis' special teams unit to lift each unit up against a Broncos team eyeing back-to-back AFC West titles, something the Chiefs won nine-straight seasons from 2016-2024.

"Yeah, absolutely. Obviously, I've learned how big of an operation this is, and how it takes a team to go win a football game," Kubiak said on what he's learned about himself 10 games into his head coaching career. "It's every week I'm learning new things. But the great thing about this whole experience is surrounding yourself with excellent people, and from our personnel staff to our coaching staff to our players, I could not have come into a better situation with the type of people."

"Yeah, it's going to be very loud. They have a great fan base, and that's something we've been practicing at practice, whether it's the crowd noise, to make sure we get adjusted to that. It's going to be a great environment," the rookie said. "But it is new. I've never started on the road before, so I'm looking forward to the challenge."

"Protection is an all 11 thing. It's everybody. The run game is an all 11 thing. That's the greatest thing about football; is every play all 11 people are involved. It's not just one person making a play. It's all 11 coming together for success. So, everybody has a role in a touchdown play. Everybody has a role in a sack. Everybody has a role in an explosive run. Everybody has a role in a tackle for loss. So, specifically, you look at each individual play and you coach every single position on how can we get better in that circumstance to make that play successful."

—Las Vegas Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko on the shared responsibility of accounting for cornerback blitzes

"Yeah, at times. We're not playing well enough. We're not playing up to the standard we need to be. So, effort covers up a lot. So, there's definitely room for improvement there. And to say it's division from the start, no, we're not playing at a high enough or good enough level right now. So, there's definitely room for improvement."

—Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard on how the fast and aggressive play style he wants from his defenders has translated into game days

#2802. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

#2800. One ‘insane’ five-minute stretch shows just how lost Mitchell Robinson is with Celtics

Mitchell Robinson looks like his heart is still in New York.

The Celtics' free-agent acquisition has looked lost in Boston this season, struggling on both ends of the floor and turning the ball over at a career-high rate.

Robinson's troubles reached a new level during a bizarre stretch Wednesday in the third quarter of an eventual 105-101 Nuggets victory.

"Robinson wasn't ready for it on the short roll," play-by-play man Mike Monaco said on the broadcast.

Boston Celtics center Mitchell Robinson, front, goes to the basket as Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic chases him on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, in Denver. AP Photo/David Zalubowski

"And I don't know if that was a great pass to Mitchell Robinson on the roll," Richard Jefferson said on the call. "I don't think that's the best place to utilize him."

The Celtics had nine turnovers in the third quarter, and while only one was credited to Robinson officially, he was involved in at least three of them.

One was an offensive foul due to a moving screen (officially given to Payton Pritchard) and two of the others were due to poor communication between him and the ball handlers.

On one sequence with six minutes remaining in the third quarter, Robinson mishandled a pick-and-roll pass, leading to a dunk at the other end for Denver.

Paul George later attempted a pass to him wide open under the basket but Robinson stopped his movement early, and the ball sailed into the stands, drawing a few comments and confused looks from George.

Then with roughly 2:40 remaining in the quarter, Robinson was switching off a cutting Christian Braun for an easy basket.

Robinson was immediately given the hook after that play, after playing roughly five minutes in a disaster quarter, with Robinson's picks heavily involved in plays that ended in turnovers.

Perhaps coach Joe Mazzulla is having a tough time figuring out how to use Robinson, as he may not be the best fit as a rim runner and pick-and-roll specialist for dunks and passes to slashers.

Boston Celtics center Mitchell Robinson has been a turnover machine this season posting career-worst numbers. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

"I think he's playing a role that we need him to play. It's bigs by committee," Mazzulla said after Monday's 115-105 loss to the Magic.

After a poor outing Monday, Robinson admitted that "I could've done better tonight."

Those watching — including Sam Vecenie, host of the basketball podcast "Game Theory" — felt a little more strongly.

"I am truly blown away by the five minutes that Mitchell Robinson played in the 3rd quarter for Boston against Denver last night," Vecenie said of Robinson. "That was insane."

Payton Pritchard and head coach Joe Mazzulla of the Boston Celtics look on during a game against the Denver Nuggets on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, in Denver. NBAE via Getty Images

Robinson's struggles go well beyond that, though. He has posted a terrible -30 plus-minus during his 246 minutes on the floor for the Celtics this year.

With him off the floor, the Celtics are +191, a massive 221-point swing.

Robinson has career-lows in rebounds per game (5.4) and an alarming 2.4 offensive rebounds per game, compared to 4.2 last year in just two fewer minutes per game for the Knicks' title team.

He's also posted a career-high 0.9 turnovers per game, and he has by far his lowest block and steal rates.

It will be interesting to see how Mazzulla gets Robinson acclimated, as he signed a three-year, $47.38 million contract this offseason. He was the one significant piece to leave the Knicks' title team as they were hellbent on not flirting with the second apron.

Celtics super fan Bill Simmons posted his concerns on X on Friday.

"'Mitchell Robinson will be fine, settle down, he just needs to play himself into shape' — a text I've sent 52 times this season already," Simmons said in a social media post.

The Celtics have been better without Mitchell Robinson on the floor. AP Photo/David Zalubowski

The Knicks have, in turn, replaced him with Andre Drummond, who is mostly there for rebounding, while former Warriors draft bust James Wiseman has also been getting some minutes at center.

The Celtics are 11-4, while the Knicks are 9-6.

LOS ANGELES – Walker Kessler let out a sigh before taking his seat at the podium at Crypto.com Arena on Friday, Nov. 20.

As much of a cliche as that saying is, it still somehow manages to encapsulate the night – or the whole week, actually – almost perfectly as the Los Angeles Lakers struggled for the third night in a row against another subpar team at home.

It took a dramatic rally and a career night from Quentin Grimes to force overtime and survive the Charlotte Hornets with a win on Tuesday. They simply looked overpowered and had no answer for the Utah Jazz on the second night of a back-to-back, losing by 12 and giving the Jazz just their third win of the season. This time, they found themselves trailing the lowly Sacramento Kings by eight at the half after sleepwalking through the first two quarters.

Head coach JJ Redick took it upon himself to motivate his players. Nobody would repeat what exactly was said but whatever it was, the messaging was received as the Lakers came back to escape yet again with a 106-104 win over the Kings.

"I can't repeat every word I used," Redick said. "The main message was we gotta be tougher, we gotta bring a little bit of energy. Certain nights, whether it's the team, how we're playing, the atmosphere in the arena, you could just be a little flat, and I thought we just had to be tougher and pick up our energy.

The Lakers' big man struggled for most of the first half, picking up four fouls that limited him to just under 12 minutes through the first two quarters. In that time, he had made just three of his six shots -- all of which came under the basket -- lacking touch on multiple finger rolls and just one rebound. Kessler said Redick laid into him in the locker room at halftime. He wasn't being physical enough. He wasn't looking to dunk the ball and was missing some touch around the rim. Defensively, he was playing undisciplined, jumping at pump fakes.

"He lit me up a little bit, and rightfully so," Kessler said. "... I needed it."

The Lakers, and Kessler, responded. They outscored the Kings 52-42 in the second half behind nine points and six rebounds from Kessler, who finished the night with a total of 15 and seven and got his plus-minus up to +4 from the -2 he had at the half.

He shot four of five from the floor in the second half, none bigger than at the start of the fourth quarter.

Collin Sexton had the ball above the three-point line, slashed to his right into the paint and dished it to his former Jazz teammate standing in the corner. Kessler put it up.

"It was a very unorganized play," Redick said. "I'm not even sure why he was standing in the corner."

The ball went through the hoop for Kessler's first three-pointer of the season on his first attempt.

"It was open," Kessler said of his reasoning for taking the shot. "I'm confident in that shot. It was open, and Bull actually told me to space because he was about to slash. ... Shot it. Went in. I feel good. I should've made those free throws (at the end), but that's part of it. It was good."

But despite the win, the Lakers' offensive struggles this week continued. Dončić had another inconsistent night shooting 3-for-8 in the second half after putting up 17 points in the first half. The team collectively shot just 35.1% from three-point range. They turned the ball over 16 times and failed to capitalize on their own takeaways early on.

Nevertheless, the Lakers took home their 14th win of the year.

"Obviously we started out not good at all," Kessler said. Me personally, I didn't play well in the first half, but I like how we responded. There's sometimes a tendency to lay down and just completely die. So it was good to see the guys fight through another tough game."

It doesn't get easier from here. The Lakers struggled against the two worst teams in the Western Conference on Wednesday and Friday. They'll have a chance to close out their homestand with a rematch against Utah on Monday before embarking on a four-game road trip that includes stops against the Memphis Grizzlies (12-4), San Antonio Spurs (13-3) and Houston Rockets (12-5).

It's not uncommon for teams to fall into the trap of playing down to the level of their competition. In a league as talented as the NBA, that can lead to some odd stretches like the one the Lakers have been on over the past week. But the team's critics have been quick to point at a perceived "soft" schedule as the driving factor behind their red-hot start that has gotten them to the first seed in the West through 17 games. They'll use these last three as evidence to support their argument, too.

The next five, however, might give a little more insight into where the Lakers really stand among their peers at this point in the season.

#2793. Badgers handle business, bounce back in major way vs. Purdue

The Wisconsin Badgers needed a strong bounce-back performance after their embarrassing loss to the Maryland Terrapins, and they got one, beating the Purdue Boilermakers 42-10 on the road on Saturday afternoon.

Wisconsin pounded the ball on the ground, going for 381 rushing yards and five rushing touchdowns, as they improved to 7-4 on the season. The loss was Purdue's second-biggest of the season behind their 39-point defeat against Notre Dame, and was a big statement from Luke Fickell's squad going into the final week of the season.

The Badgers started the game with the ball and instantly controlled the pace, going 14 plays for 75 yards and a touchdown on a drive lasting nearly seven minutes to open things up. Wisconsin converted three third downs and a fourth down on the drive, capping things off with a 24-yard Eugene Hilton rushing touchdown.

They quickly forced a three-and-out and were back on the offensive, once again slowly moving the ball down the field before Colton Joseph broke off for a 32-yard rushing touchdown, his first of a few in the game.

Purdue looked like it was heading to another three-and-out, but converted a fourth down, and a Wisconsin penalty was enough for them to get into field goal range. They stalled out on the next set of plays and kicked a 53-yard field goal.

That score was short-lived as the Badgers went two plays and 75 yards for their third touchdown of the game. Jacob Harris had a long 26-yard catch-and-run to start the drive before Darrion Dupree went 49 yards to the house for a 21-3 lead.

That's when Purdue was finally able to respond with some life offensively. The Boilermakers went pass-heavy and slowly moved the ball through the air before Ryan Browne hit Cooper McCutchan for a 24-yard catch, getting Purdue inside the five-yard line, where they punched it in three plays later on a direct snap to Fame Ijeboi.

Wisconsin's offense had its first punt of the day with a three-and-out, and Purdue was once again able to slowly move the ball, getting two first downs, including one from a Jai'mier Scott hold. But three straight incompletions forced Purdue to punt it back to the Badgers with 2:43 left in the first half.

And Wisconsin looked to make the most of the opportunity, as Colton Joseph went for 19 yards on the first play of the drive, getting the Badgers out from deep inside their own territory. The Badgers picked up another first down and a personal foul set them up in striking range at the Purdue 34-yard line. But a major negative play on second down, a loss of 12, killed the drive for the Badgers, taking them out of field goal range and costing them a final scoring chance before the half ended.

The Boilermakers got the ball to start the second half, but quickly gave it up with a three-and-out after a holding penalty on first down. And the Badgers got to work on the ground. This time, the Badgers went 12 plays for 74 yards and a touchdown, going with nine runs and three passes for a Darrion Dupree one-yard touchdown.

However, a couple of key plays on the drive came through the air. On 3rd & 7, Colton Joseph hit Chris Brooks for a first-down conversion, extending the drive. Joseph had another 11-yard hit to Jaylon Domingeaux and a key 20-yard completion to Domingeaux on 3rd & 2 to set Wisconsin up at the two-yard line.

Suddenly, it was 28-10 Badgers with Wisconsin in full control.

Wisconsin's defense continued its superb day, forcing another punt after one first down, with another holding penalty killing the Boilermakers. Then, the offensive onslaught on the ground continued, with the Badgers rushing 11 times and throwing just twice on their following drive, resulting in an 11-play, 85-yard touchdown drive.

Colton Joseph had a carry for 23, Darrion Dupree had an 18-yard run, and Joseph had another 22-yard run to keep Wisconsin in scoring position before Eugene Hilton hit Joseph for a 13-yard touchdown pass on a trick play to send the Badgers up 35-10.

Purdue, struggling for explosives, caught a break with a pass interference call to start its next drive, and they were able to get two first downs while slowly moving the ball. But, once again failing to make a big play, the Boilermakers were stuck with a 2nd & 5 on Wisconsin's 34 and had three straight incompletions to force a turnover on downs.

Colton Joseph called game from there, taking the first play 66 yards to the house to seal the deal for the Badgers with a 42-10 blowout, and the game ended that way, marking a huge win for Luke Fickell's squad after a poor outing last weekend.

Wisconsin's defense held Purdue to under 200 yards of offense, while the offense went for over 500 in the big win.

Next up, the Badgers cap their season off against the Minnesota Gophers, looking to reclaim the Axe for the first time in three years.

#2791. Jaguars saw something in Liam Coen that other teams didn't

In a season and a half with the Jaguars, Liam Coen has established himself as one of the best coaches in the NFL. Last year, Coen took over a team that had gone 4-13 the year before and improved their record to 13-4 — the best record ever for a first-year coach taking over a team that had won four or fewer games the year before. This year Coen is showing that last year was no fluke, with the Jaguars at 7-2 with an NFL-best point differential of +125.

Coen’s great success should have other teams that hired new head coaches in 2025 asking themselves: What did we miss? Because the Jaguars were so high on Coen that he was their No. 1 target and they were willing to do whatever it took to get him, while no other team even bothered to give Coen an interview.

During the 2025 NFL coaching search, we tracked dozens of reports of head coaching interviews and requests among the seven teams that had vacancies. The Jaguars were the only team that so much as asked Coen to interview.

This week there’s been some media scrutiny on the Jets, who hired Aaron Glenn without considering Coen as a candidate. Glenn is 5-22; Coen is 20-6. But it’s unfair to single out the Jets for failing to interview Coen, because no team other than the Jaguars did, either.

The 41-year-old Coen had a résumé that should have made him a good candidate. NFL teams are always on the lookout for coaches who can nurture a franchise quarterback and run an innovative offense. Coen played quarterback at UMass and coached quarterbacks in college before getting hired by Sean McVay to work on the Rams’ staff, eventually became the Rams’ offensive coordinator under McVay, and had been a successful playcaller as offensive coordinator for the Buccaneers, as well as at Kentucky. With that background, it’s surprising that only the Jaguars wanted him.

And the Jaguars really wanted him, to the point that they were willing to do whatever it took to hire him. Coen initially turned the Jaguars down and agreed to a contract extension to stay with the Buccaneers, but Jaguars owner Shad Khan wouldn’t take no for an answer. When Coen said he was concerned about the direction of the Jaguars’ front office, Khan fired General Manager Trent Baalke and agreed to reshape the front office in a way that Coen would approve of if Coen would take the job. Coen was persuaded to take the Jaguars job, and the Jaguars later hired James Gladstone, who had worked with Coen on the Rams, as GM.

The result has been the Jaguars going from one of the worst teams in the NFL to one of the best. Coen’s success in Jacksonville has justified the faith Khan had in him. And raises questions about the total lack of interest from the rest of the league.

New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith (7) runs the ball against the Buffalo Bills at MetLife Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Charles Wenzelberg/NY Post

#2787. Billie Jean King honored with handprint ceremony at Hollywood's TCL Chinese Theatre

Tennis legend Billie Jean King Thursday became the first American-born woman athlete honored with a handprint-footprint ceremony at the TCL Chinese Theatre.

"I sincerely hope I'm not the last," King said in her acceptance speech. "My parents and my brother, who have passed, would be so happy today if they were here, and they would remind me this is a really big deal."

King's brother, Randy Moffitt, was a relief pitcher for three major league teams from 1972-83. He died in 2025 in Long Beach following a long illness at age 76.

King also recalled childhood trips with her family from Long Beach to what was to then Grauman's Chinese Theatre "to walk among historic hand and footprints."

"It was very exciting," King said. "We watched ceremonies on the local TV news. We talked about it at the dinner table. Our family really loved this world, and because of that, today is very special for me. "

The other woman athlete honored in the theater's forecourt at 6925 Hollywood Blvd. is the Norwegian-born three-time gold medal-winning figure skater Sonja Henie, who imprinted her ice skates at her 1937 ceremony.

King's ceremony was the final handprint-footprint event in the forecourt before the historic theater celebrates its 100th anniversary in 2027, according to organizers.

In the era before Thursday's computerized rankings, experts selected the Long Beach Poly High School graduate as the world's No. 1 women's tennis player from 1966-68, 1971-72 and 1974. She won 39 Grand Slam titles -- 12 in singles, 16 in doubles and 11 in mixed doubles.

She led the "Original 9" women players who signed $1 contracts in 1970 to launch the first major women's professional tennis tour, challenging the sport's disparity in prize money.

King helped found the Women's Tennis Association three years later.

Her victory over Bobby Riggs in the 1973 "Battle of the Sexes" remains one of the best-known events in sports history. That same year, the U.S. Open became the first major sporting event to award equal prize money to men and women.

King was also among the founders of World TeamTennis, the first co-ed professional sports league. In 1971, she became the first woman athlete to earn $100,000 in a year.

Last year, she became the first woman honored with a Hollywood Walk of Fame star in the sports entertainment category, which was created in 2021 to recognize athletes who have made significant contributions to entertainment.

King was honored in part for serving as an executive producer of the 2023 PBS documentary series "Groundbreakers," which paired legendary women athletes with current stars.

Her other entertainment credits include serving as an executive producer of the 2013 documentary "The Battle of the Sexes," along with appearances as herself on "Fresh Off the Boat," "Arli$$" and "The Odd Couple."

In a recent Guardian interview, King said she kept quiet about her sexuality early in her career because she feared the women's tour would lose sponsorships.

"This is when it's not about yourself sometimes," King said. "It's about the future of the sport."

King publicly came out in 1981 after being outed, and she said she lost every endorsement overnight.

In 2009, King became the first woman athlete to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom, recognizing her advocacy for women and the LGBTQ+ community.

She also founded the Women's Sports Foundation and the Billie Jean King Foundation, which support girls, women and future leaders through sports, education and activism.

Her documentary, "Give Me the Ball!," will premiere Sunday on ESPN, the ESPN App and Disney+ in the United States.

The ESPN Films documentary, directed by Liz Garbus and Elizabeth Wolff, includes archival footage and interviews with King, Serena Williams, Elton John and Chris Evert.

Note: teams are permitted to temporarily elevate up to two practice squad players per game. A player can be elevated up to three times in the regular season and an unlimited number of times in the postseason.

#2776. Hawks excel off of turnovers, eliminate Hornets in NBA Cup win

The Atlanta Hawks picked up another victory in the NBA Cup on Friday night, eliminating the Charlotte Hornets from cup progression with a 111-97 victory at State Farm Arena. Jalen Johnson led the Hawks with 26 points while Aaron Wiggins added 19 points. For the Hornets, Moussa Diabate scored 21 points, Brandon Miller added 19 points.

After suffering a disappointing loss to the Bulls in overtime in their last NBA Cup appearance, the Hawks were presented a good opportunity to steady their position in the standings with a home tie against a struggling Charlotte side. Naturally, it was the visitors who were in the ascendancy for the majority of the first half. Rallying behind their size, the Hornets secured 12 offensive rebounds leading to 20 second chance points in the first half alone, contributing to the Hornets taking not just double-digit lead in the second quarter but a lead that ran as high as 14 points.

"Diabate was part of it," said Hawks head coach Quin Snyder of the Hornets' rebounding prowess. "Not only do they have he and Kalkbrenner, two guys that it's very difficult to keep them off glass by yourself. If you are able to put a second body on, which we didn't do enough. When we did, he may not get it, but then everybody's got to clean it up. The first part of that, we need to do better. The second part of it, I'd like to get to the second part where he actually doesn't get it (the rebound). A credit to him as far as how relentless he is on the glass. I thought as the game went on, we had some possessions, and those would be guard rebounds. I think RayJ got five (rebounds), he's the smallest guy on the court. We've got to have everybody in the mix to be effective on the defensive glass."

A cold stretch from the Hornets allowed the Hawks the opportunity to chip away at the lead; by the end of which the Hawks had whittled the lead down to just two points heading into the locker room. This momentum carried through into the second half, with the Hawks not only to re-take the lead but established a double-digit lead by the end of the third quarter, progressing to a lead as high as 19 points in the fourth quarter. While a Hornets run briefly brought the lead down to 10 points, it never dipped below double-digits and the Hawks would go on to secure a comfortable victory.

Postgame, Snyder was asked about the Hornets being limited to 40 second half points, and outlined the details that the Hawks tightened up on in the second half.

"I think our rotations were not sharp early, we were just a step behind," said Snyder of the second half. "That's really important for us in our pick-and-roll defense. As we're trying to keep the ball out of the paint, we're going to find ourselves in those situations. Some of it was close-outs, when we switched pick-and-roll we weren't aggressive enough early. They shot just right behind the screen. I just think we weren't as sharp as we needed to be."

One of the keys to victory in this contest were the Hawks' points off of turnovers, scoring 36 off of the Hornets' 17 turnovers.

On the drive and pass in the air from Coby White, Dyson Daniels pounces on the loose pass, and shovels the ball ahead to Nickeil Alexander-Walker for the basket:

On this drive, it's Jalen Johnson who comes up with the knockaway, and leads the break himself in transition to dunk at the rim:

Here, Moussa Diabate operates looking for a hand-off, and his pass is telegraphed by Aaron Wiggins, who escapes Naz Reid to finish at the rim:

Again, the Hawks are active on the perimeter and Daniels procures another steal and hands it off to Alexander-Walker, who pitches it to Johnson, who finishes at the rim again:

RayJ Dennis and Zuby Ejiofor combine on this defensive play to produce another Hornets turnover, from which Dennis gets into his runner for another basket in the third quarter:

Another knock-away from Dennis sets up another Atlanta fastbreak, this time Dennis lifts the alley-oop to Ejiofor for a highlight play:

With Kingston Flemings, Jock Landale, Asa Newell, and Mo Gueye absent, there were opportunities that may not normally be available for RayJ Dennis and Zuby Ejiofor. Both players made meaningful impacts in their time on the court, and we've looked at a few already with the turnovers.

Ejiofor played 13 minutes and scored five points, but his impact goes beyond the boxscore as Snyder outlined postgame.

"I think it's timely as well," said Snyder of Ejiofor's energy off the bench. "There's plays, whether it's a block— you see him dunk but what you don't notice all the time is he sprinted to get to that position. Those are the things ,in my mind, that are hard, because he's running without the promise of a reward. Sometimes for gratification, it's hard. The things that our team needs to do to be good, that's consistent, there's not a payout in the moment. You have to run, even when you don't get the ball, you have to get a hit, even when you don't get the rebound, you have to space, even if you don't get the shot. Those things are important to him. As a result, he puts himself in position to make those kinds of plays. It's the combination of the two things together because what he's doing is selfless, and then he actually gets rewarded for it. It's a really good thing. It's something we talk about and I want our whole team to emulate.When we do it, we're a much better team."

The play Snyder was referring to, I believe, is this one, where Ejiofor runs the floor and receives the pass for the dunk in transition:

Ejiofor did not back down when confronted with Diabate while on the floor; it was this, in addition to the energy he provided, that stood out to the Hawks last night.

"It was good, rook coming in, you know, not backing down," said Dyson Daniels of Ejiofor. "It's what we like, another big fella getting the mix with Mo (Gueye) being out, that's usually Mo doing that sort of thing. So, Zuby in there, it was really cool to see. He's just come in, giving us really good minutes, giving us good energy around the floor, and he's making some big shots for us. He's really stepped up since Jock's gone down, which has been good."

Dennis, similarly, played 13 minutes, scoring eight points but, similar to Ejiofor, his impact was felt beyond his boxscore.

"It's great when you have guys in the program," said Snyder of RayJ Dennis. "Last year in College Park, this summer, throughout the course of September, he's got a good feel for how we want to play. He played well in Oklahoma City, is all he didn't make a shot. He can get in the lane and when he gets in there he's capable of finishing. He also has good vision, I think he's worked on that, too. Big minutes from him tonight gave us a lift."

Without CJ McCollum and and Kingston Flemings in the lineup, the Hawks have been operating without a primary point guard. It was Dyson Daniels who stepped up with 10 assists last night to lead the Hawks from a playmaking perspective. Daniels himself believe it has been done by committee.

"I think everyone's stepped up," said Daniels of the point guard play without McCollum and Flemings. "Obviously, we don't have like Kingston or CJ, like a true point guard out there but we've just been pushing the pace. Everyone's getting touches, we've got guys that can play with the ball, guys that can play off the ball. So I think everyone's just filled those voids. Guys like RayJ (Dennis) have been really good coming in as well, playing, some good minutes for us. Corey (Kispert) coming as well, playing some really good minutes. Everyone's kind of stepped up, which has been good."

While Daniels starred in his own role, there was little doubt as to who the MVP was for the Hawks last night, and that was Jalen Johnson. Johnson scored 26 points on 10-of-15 shooting from the field and 3-of-4 from three:

As we looked at earlier, Johnson excelled in transition/off of Charlotte turnovers. The manner of which he was able to manoeuvre through bodies in transition to get to the rim looked effortless at times; he just looked in total command in the open court.

It hasn't been an easy season for Johnson shooting the three-pointer, shooting 22% on the season, and while it was encouraging to see Johnson hit 3-of-4 from, the poor percentages so far are't going to dissuade the Hawks and Johnson from shooting.

"I think he knows that we want him to keep shooting," said Snyder of Johnson. "The catch-and-shoots that he hit were quick decisions. I thought the thing that he did tonight where he was really impactful was he played without the ball. That's important for him and for us, particularly when people are game-planning for him, whether it was a matchup on the ball, his ability to do both, to get out in transition, to get to the foul line, to offensive rebound, all those things add up. I think it calms your nervous system a little bit, too. He knows how we feel about him. His shooting the ball is important for us, so it's good to see a couple go in, no question about it. I don't want to obsess about it either because there's lots of ways he can help us."

"I mean it happens," added Johnson of his three-point shooting. "Obviously I haven't shot the ball the way I wanted to but I put in the work. I'm not worried about the percentage or whatnot, I know my shot is going to fall. It was good to see a couple go in for sure. I'm going to keep shooting the shots that I work on and just continue to let them fall."

The Hawks move to 2-1 in the NBA Cup and are currently 2nd in the group, trailing the Boston Celtics who have played just two cup games (2-0). The Hawks and Celtics will face-off next Friday at the TD Garden, the winner practically guaranteed to advance from Group C. The Hawks are obviously motivated to win, but the mechanisms of the NBA Cup provide another incentive to win.

"I mean, obviously we want that money," said Jalen Johnson when asked how the Hawks prepare for a cup game. "So, I think it's as simple as that. Obviously we understand that the stakes are higher considering what's for the reward. So, I think we all young, we all like an extra prize and money. So, I think just upping our intensity, upping our focus."

The Hawks (10-6) are back in action on Sunday afternoon where they host the Detroit Pistons (10-5) at State Farm Arena.

#2772. FINAL: Boston College Takes Down Syracuse 27-15

Boston College leaned on its running game and a bend-but-don't-break defense to beat Syracuse 27-15. Bo MacCormack supplied the explosive runs with 236 yards on 30 carries, while the Eagles repeatedly turned Syracuse big-play scoring opportunities into field goals, or nothing at all.

It was not always comfortable, but BC made the plays that mattered. MacCormack broke loose for a 56-yard touchdown in the third quarter, then delivered another long run to set up a crucial fourth-quarter score. On the other side, the Eagles surrendered too many big passing plays but repeatedly held their ground near the goal line. It's been a problem for this Syracuse team all season, and reared its ugly head again. Nice when it's not us!

BC could hardly have scripted a better opening possession. Mason McKenzie found Javarius Green for 22 yards, MacCormack ripped off a 47-yard run, and McKenzie capped the four-play, 81-yard drive with a six-yard touchdown pass to tight end Zeke Moore.

The defense had a solid start as well despite allowing a big play to Calvin Russell III. The freshman helped get them to the BC five but the defense held strong and forced a field goal.

That inability to finish drives became a recurring theme. Syracuse's receivers created problems downfield, and BC let the Orange escape several third-and-long situations. The Eagles had their own missed opportunities. A Syracuse targeting penalty extended a possession, but McKenzie missed an open Moore for a potential touchdown, leaving BC to settle for a field goal and a 10-3 lead. Syracuse then appeared to answer with a touchdown, only for the play to be wiped out, and the BC defense got the full stop on fourth down.

The Eagles finished the half with a well-executed late possession, setting up a field goal on the final play to take a 13-3 advantage into the locker room.

Syracuse chipped away with long third-quarter field goal, to cut the lead to 13-9. That came after quarterback Steve Angeli got knocked out of the game after a hit by Demetrius Ballard and Malachi Nelson took over

For a stretch, both teams struggled to generate much of anything. Stalled possessions and poor punting slowed the game down and kept things tight.

Then MacCormack broke it open. His 56-yard touchdown run gave BC a 20-9 temporary cushion. Syracuse responded with a long touchdown pass to Umari Hatcher. The superstar wideout had over 200 yards in the game. BC stopped the two-point attempt, keeping the margin at 20-15. Another big play to Hatcher put Syracuse in position to cut further into the lead, but a missed field goal now kept it at five. MacCormack promptly seized the moment, breaking another long run to the Syracuse 20 and setting up the touchdown that brought back BC's two-score advantage.

From there it was one more Eagles red-zone stop to finish the job. BC did not need a flawless afternoon to get a badly neede win. BC heads to Miami to close out the season, with the longest of long shots to get a bowl game (unless an academic 5 win bowl has already been achieved).

The sudden decision of the NFL to suspend receiver Puka Nacua three games raises plenty of relevant questions. On Friday, a technically irrelevant question was answered.

After Rams coach Sean McVay disclosed to reporters that Nacua had surgery to repair a torn MCL suffered during a Week 9 win over the Commanders, Judy Battista of NFL Network reported this: “The NFL did not know Puka Nacua had had knee surgery on Tuesday when it suspended him yesterday.”

Surely, that’s accurate; Judy is a solid reporter. But that extra fact doesn’t matter to the NFL’s ultimate handling of Nacua.

The report creates the impression that, during the negotiations that resulted in the three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua and/or his representatives withheld material information. That, at some level, the league had been duped by the lack of knowledge that Nacua had undergone surgery that will sideline him for “a couple months.”

First, the suspension (as the league affirmatively explained on Thursday) is separate from the injury. The NFL listed multiple examples of players who served suspensions while injured.

Second, whether Nacua (who had already missed one of the four minimum games he’s required to miss while on IR), was already going to serve the entirety of the suspension while on injured reserve with or without surgery.

Third, the surgery and the extended absence actually avoids the possibility that Nacua would have returned to action exactly one game after finishing his suspension, resulting in no net games missed due to the suspension.

The mere existence of the report represents an implicit acknowledgement by the league that the negotiated suspension, aimed at allowing Nacua to double-dip when it comes to his stint on injured reserve and his suspension, underscores the broader question of whether players should be allowed to serve a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy when otherwise unable to play. That’s a separate issue for the NFL to revisit, if it chooses, through a potential revision to the terms of the policy.

As explained on Friday, the league could have refused the deal. It could have insisted on pushing the issue through the full process, with Judge Sue L. Robinson conducting a hearing and the outcome potentially being appealed (by Nacua and/or the league) to the Commissioner. But that would have entailed a non-zero-percent chance that Nacua wouldn’t have been suspended at all.

For Nacua, the goal was to get the suspension served while injured. The fact that he had surgery before the agreement was reached gave him more of a buffer than the NFL knew about, expanding the window during which the suspension could be fully served before the end of the 2026 season without Nacua missing time due to the suspension. Which would still allow Nacua to have this issue behind him before the 2027 offseason, when he signs a new contract with the Rams, has the franchise tag applied, or becomes a free agent.

Of course, Nacua now needs to tread lightly. The league has made it clear that “any further violation of the Personal Conduct Policy, including failing to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program, will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the League.” To the extent that the league isn’t thrilled by the perception/reality that it allowed Nacua to serve his suspension at a time when he otherwise could not play, the league could be ready to pounce on any opportunity to impose a longer suspension that would apply when Nacua is healthy again.

#2767. Avalanche Linked to Sidney Crosby, but Have a Major Problem

It had been an open secret. But now it's official. It's coming down to the Montreal Canadiens and Colorado Avalanche in the Sidney Crosby sweepstakes.

The door is now officially open in Pittsburgh.

Kyle Dubas sent a very clear message Wednesday: the Penguins are ready to make moves. With a 7-11-2 record and the team sitting near the bottom of the Eastern Conference standings, the general manager has announced a fire sale.

He wants trades focused on the future, bringing in young players who can contribute to the next version of the Penguins. And in the middle of all this, there's obviously Sidney Crosby.

The captain is set to become an unrestricted free agent on July 1. If Pittsburgh decides to move him before then, Crosby himself would have to agree to a trade to a contender.

Dubas acknowledged that he had spoken with his veteran players about the organization's situation and what could happen over the coming weeks. He also emphasized his tremendous respect for Crosby and said he would respect whatever decision the captain makes.

In a nutshell, Pittsburgh will trade him to whichever team he wants.

In an article published in the Toronto Sun, Bruce Garrioch identified the two potential destinations that could battle for the legendary forward: Colorado and Montreal.

On the Avalanche's side, Nathan MacKinnon is Crosby's best friend. The idea of bringing the two superstars together in the same uniform would obviously be incredibly appealing. MacKinnon would certainly love to have his close friend alongside him as they try to win another Stanley Cup.

But Colorado has a major problem: its available assets. The Avalanche have already sacrificed a significant number of draft picks and young players to build their current roster.

They don't own their first-round picks in 2027 or 2028. Their prospect pool is also extremely limited, and when you look at the organization's top 10 young players, it's easy to understand why Pittsburgh would never accept an offer from Colorado.

The first name is goaltender Ilya Nabokov, a 23-year-old playing for the Colorado Eagles in the AHL. Selected 38th overall in 2024, he possesses excellent mobility and impressive athleticism.

He enjoyed three strong seasons in the KHL before moving to North America. He's an interesting prospect, but Pittsburgh doesn't need another young goaltender, especially with Sergei Murashov already viewed as part of the Penguins' future.

The second is Egor Shilov, an 18-year-old center selected 43rd overall in 2026. He scored 32 goals and recorded 82 points with the Victoriaville Tigres in the Quebec Maritimes Junior Hockey League. His offensive talent is undeniable, but his pace of play and certain deficiencies away from the puck raise questions about his development.

Beckett Hamilton, another 18-year-old center, ranks third. Selected in the third round in 2026, he scored 24 goals and recorded 62 points in 67 games with the Red Deer Rebels. He has good speed, likes to shoot, and has shown promising offensive skills. He's an intriguing young player, but remains a lower-tier prospect who needs further development.

The fourth is goaltender Tobiáš Tvrzník, an 18-year-old selected in the fourth round in 2026. At 6-foot-4 with good athleticism, he has some interesting tools. However, he's still a goaltender who is a long way from the NHL.

Fifth is left-handed defenseman Mikhail Gulyayev, a 21-year-old selected 31st overall in 2023. He has excellent mobility, but his development is concerning. His playing time in Omsk in the KHL has been limited.

Colorado has a massive competitive advantage with Nathan MacKinnon, but Montreal has the assets to put together a much more complete offer for Kyle Dubas.

The Toronto Sun has now put Montreal and Colorado at the center of the conversation. Crosby will give his GM the opportunity to choose between the two teams.

#2759. Flour Bluff volleyball seniors leave mark after second state title match

Flour Bluff and Highland Park came into this week as the last two UIL state champions in Class 5A Division I volleyball in the state, and both showed their championship meddle in the 2026 title game.

Pushed to the brink in each of the first two sets, the Scots found a way to erase multiple set points and will themselves to a 2-0 lead.

But like any team with championship pedigree, the Hornets showed the grit that allowed them to earn their way to the Curtis Culwell Center for the second time in three years, battling back to force a decisive fifth set, before the Scots emerged with a 27-25, 28-26, 22-25, 20-25, 15-12 win.

FLOUR BLUFF VOLLEYBALL: Flour Bluff volleyball falls in five sets to Highland Park in UIL title game

The Hornets and nine seniors saw their aim of a second state title in three years fall a few points short, ending as the state runner up after another dominant season.

Flour Bluff (37-11) had won 60 straight sets going into the championship match as part of a 20-game win streak, including sweeps in both the regional final against Sharyland and state semifinal against Georgetown.

The Scots, which claimed back-to-back state titles with the win, had a height advantage with three players taller than 6-foot-2, but the Hornets controlled the majority of all five sets. Highland Park needed late surges in all three sets they claimed, to hoist the trophy.

"We dug deep," Flour Bluff head coach Kara Wallace said. "A lot of people would probably say that team was better than us, but we came in and showed them what South Texas was about. I don't think there is anything for them to hang their head over. They gave them an amazing game.

"How can you be mad if you go five sets with anyone? I'm super proud of the leadership that I had from them. They stepped up and they fought back after we could have keeled over after those first two sets."

Flour Bluff led 24-21 in the first set only to see the Scots rattled off a 6-1 run and then had another lead at 24-23 in the second before Highland Park surged late.

Kristina Rodriguez helped the Hornets late in the third to close out the set, while Nya White and Emily Eggleston had strong fourth sets as Flour Bluff pushed the match to five.

"I told them to trust each other, believe in each other, have heart and have faith," said Wallace of her message during the changeover after the second set. "That is what got us here — working as a family and a team.

"We figured out what was working for us, shook off some of the nerves and we were ready to settle in. We had a lot of kids step up in places we really needed."

White, a Texas State signee, led all players with 20 kills in the championship match while Alyssa Thornton (UT Tyler commit) recorded 10 kills. Rodriguez (St. Mary's) excelled in multiple areas with nine kills, 25 assists and 12 digs.

Rodriguez explained how tight-knit the team is and how much representing Flour Bluff has been for her.

"A lot of us have played multiple seasons together for years," Rodriguez said. "When we wear Flour Bluff across our chest, it is not just the school, it is the community, our teammates and our sisters along with us."

Wallace said it will be challenging to replace a large, highly successful senior group, but the mark they have left will last.

"They've been with me a long time. Some of these kids have played with me for four years straight," Wallace said. "It is going to be big shoes to fill. They are leaving behind a huge legacy and tradition. These kids have been able to go to state twice in three years, which is incredible for us.

"I am going to miss them a lot. They are like my kids. My daughters. We laugh. We cry. I crash out on them but then we come back together and its ok. We love each other. We have a lot to fill for next year, for sure."

This article originally appeared on Corpus Christi Caller Times: Flour Bluff volleyball seniors leave mark after second state title match

#2755. Will Shane Steichen be back in 2027?

After the 2025 season ended, Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon put both G.M. Chris Ballard and coach Shane Steichen on notice that much was expected in 2026.

Then, one day after the Colts lost to the Titans in Week 6, she fired Ballard and kept Steichen.

Nearly five weeks later, Steichen remains. After next Sunday’s game against the Giants, the Colts will enter their bye. That’s typically the best time for an in-season coaching change, since it gives the interim coach maximum time to get up to speed before the next game.

Creating a vacancy with six weeks left in the regular season carries a separate benefit. The team can get a head start on searching for the replacement. And if ownership already knows the coach will be fired after the season ends, it makes no sense to delay that part of the process.

So here’s the question. Will Irsay-Gordon bring Steichen back in 2027?

It makes no sense to keep a new G.M. from hiring a new coach. Every G.M. arrives with a wish list of coaches who would be pursued, if/when the position is vacant. It makes plenty of sense to give a new G.M. an immediate vacancy to fill.

But what about the Colts this year has made sense? The firing of the G.M. left the team without a seasoned, experienced executive to navigate the strategy of making, or not making, trades. They quickly moved guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. They rejected offers for running back Jonathan Taylor and quarterback Daniel Jones. They moved two starting receivers — Keenan Allen and Josh Downs — on the day of the trade deadline.

Steichen has been operating for much of the season with one hand tied behind his back. Now, he’ll have both wrists secured. Whatever the decision will be as to Steichen, it’s unfair to base it on the team’s overall performance since the Nelson and Buckner trades.

Before that point, they took the Chiefs to overtime in Kansas City. They beat the Texans. They manhandled the Commanders in London. They took the Vikings to the limit in Minnesota.

Although the signs point to Steichen eventually being fired, the fact that he’s still there now means he could still be there later. The new G.M. may be expected to work with him.

It’s ultimately the owner’s call. And the owner may have strong feelings about Steichen’s skills and abilities, based on the fact that she’s on the sideline every week.

If she was upstairs, she’d likely be hearing criticism of the head coach during the game. Instead, she’s watching him in his element. And she hasn’t fired him yet.

Throw in the fact that a new coach may not be as welcoming to the owner’s presence in the bench area, and she may be even more inclined to give Steichen (who’s fine with it) another chance. Especially since she systematically began making his job much more difficult the moment the Colts traded Nelson and Buckner.

Moving forward, it’ll be virtually impossible. The fact that Steichen has survived this long could mean that he’ll survive whatever comes next.

#2753. Florida football WR Eric Singleton Jr mum about future after breakout game

Florida football redshirt junior Eric Singleton Jr has played most of the 2026 season through a high ankle sprain he suffered on the seventh play of the season in Week 1 against Florida Atlantic.

Against Vanderbilt, the 5-foot-10, 184-pond Singleton finally displayed the tantalizing promise he showed during spring and fall drills with the Florida Gators.

Singleton finished with six catches for 117 yards during UF's 34-27 win over the Commodores, including a key fourth catch in the fourth quarter that required some luck and concentration.

With the score tied at 27, Florida quarterback Aaron Philo fired a pass over the middle that deflected off the hands of receiver Micah Mays and then helicoptered into the hands of Singleton, who ran another 10 yards to complete a 37-yard pass play.

A Vanderbilt roughing the passer penalty against Philo moved the ball down to the Vandy 10-yard line, and on the next play, Jadan Baugh scored a 10-yard TD run to give UF a 34-27 lead it wouldn't relinquish.

"I'm never going to be above taking some luck," Florida coach Jon Sumrall said. "We got some today on that play. I'm happy for E. The year in a lot of ways on his individual performance hasn't gone the way any of us probably predicted or would have thought. He's worked his tail off."

Earlier in the game, Singleton also caught a 50-yard pass from Philo in the second quarter. which set up UF's first TD of the game, a Philo 1-yard TD run.

"That's something I've been emphasizing with Philo," Singleton said. "I don't care about the post safety being there, he's still got me because I can still run by him. He gave me a shot today and I made a play."

An Auburn transfer, Singleton could have walked on Senior Day before UF's win over Vanderbilt but didn't. As a fourth-year player who began his career at Georgia Tech, Singleton still has one year of eligibility left under the NCAA's new five-for-five rule.

Singleton said at this point he's unsure whether he will declare for the NFL draft or return to school.

"I haven't really made any kind of decision," Singleton said. "I'm just trying to finish this season."

Singleton entered the 2026 season as the fastest player on UF's roster, running a peak speed of 23 miles per hour. The ankle injury robbed him of some of that breakaway playmaking ability, but he said he's feeling closer to 100 percent each week.

"Obviously it hasn't gone the way I wanted it to, dealt a big injury early on," Singleton said. "But I think God has a plan for me and it's coming to light now, and I think everything is going to fall in line for me."

Kevin Brockway is The Gainesville Sun's Florida beat writer. Contact him at kbrockway@gannett.com. Follow him on X @KevinBrockwayG1.

#2751. Walker Kessler flashes ‘f–k yeah’ moment in game of ‘f–k nos’

As Walker Kessler walked into the interview room, he uttered four words.

The Lakers, who have the NBA's best record at 14-3, had eked past the Kings (1-14), who are in the league's cellar.

Walker Kessler (14) of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots a 3-point basket against the Sacramento Kings on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

For Kessler, the Lakers' 106-104 win on Friday was mostly forgettable.

He got lit into by Lakers coach JJ Redick at halftime after only having six points and one rebound before turning things around to finish with 15 points, seven rebounds and three blocked shots. He missed two free throws with 5.3 seconds left and the Lakers up, 106-104, a blemish that would've been much worse had Zach LaVine not missed his go-ahead 3-point attempt with 0.9 seconds left.

In a few days, no one is going to remember that the Lakers trailed the Kings by as much as 11 points in a game with 10 lead changes and 15 ties. All that anyone is going to remember is the W.

Kessler has already proven himself as an excellent rim defender and rebounder, but on Friday he revealed that there are some more tricks in his bag.

With 11:42 remaining in the fourth quarter and the Lakers trailing the Kings, 84-82, Collin Sexton passed the ball to the 7-foot-1 center in the corner. Kessler then fired a 24-foot jumper which swished through the net.

Dylan Cardwell of the Sacramento Kings plays defense on Walker Kessler of the Los Angeles Lakers in Los Angeles, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Walker Kessler grabs a rebound during the NBA Cup game at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

So in a game with so many "F–k nos," Kessler finally got his moment.

"I feel good," Kessler said, adding a caveat. "Should've made those free throws."
