#2749. Raiders owner Mark Davis hated the Madden movie

The new Madden movie includes a brief, fleeting glance of a young Mark Davis. The depiction wasn’t flattering.

His assessment of the film is far less flattering.

The Raiders owner teed off on the Madden movie, in an interview with John Katsolimetes of the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

“My comment is, it’s full of turducken,” Davis said initially.

“It depends on whether you like turducken or not, and obviously, I don’t like turducken,” Davis said.

“I think it’s really it’s unfair to take people that have passed away and make caricatures out of them, and try to sell it as truth,” Davis said. “They start the movie with a statement saying that all of it’s not true, but some of it is, so it’s confusing what to believe.”

That’s not an uncommon device. “Based on a true story” means that plenty of liberties will be taken in an effort to make the story more compelling.

Mark Davis had one specific concern regarding the shading of the truth. He objected to his father’s reaction to the serious neck injury suffered by Patriots receiver Darryl Stingley, during a preseason game in 1978.

“So John goes over to the hospital afterwards, you know, and really looks after him,” Mark Davis said, “and there’s a scene where my dad is telling John, ‘You don’t need to go over there. You don’t need to take care of other teams’ players. You take care of our players.’

“That’s just so far from the truth. Anybody who has ever known him knows my dad always took care of people behind the scenes. If it was a player from another team had an issue that wasn’t being taken care of, my dad would quietly take care of that even if it was players on other teams. I’m serious. . . . It just it felt cheap to me to build up John’s image at the expense of my father’s.”

Davis praised Christian Bale for his portrayal of Al Davis.

“You can’t blame the script on him,” Mark Davis said. “He tried.”

Mark Davis also didn’t care for the characterization of the iconic John Madden by Nicolas Cage.

“You know, he at times did look like John, but he wasn’t John,” Davis said. “I mean, they made John to be a pussy, and John was the farthest thing from a pussy.”

The end result could be a positive. Mark Davis is now motivated to create something that properly and accurately depicts his father.

“I don’t know what this movie’s purpose was, to be honest,” Mark Davis said. “But you know, it’s making me more and more realize that I’m going to have to put together something on my dad. It could be a movie, it could be a characterization, but at least it’ll be truthful. . . .

“I think I need to do that, or at least let people know that I’m thinking about doing that, so that don’t jump in and think that they can do it first.”

The concerns expressed by Mark Davis regarding the script raise the question of whether he or the league or anyone bothered to review it before allowing the producers to use the Raiders name, colors, and logos in the filming of the football sequences. That’s a critical aspect when it comes to the overall credibility of a film about pro football.

If it looks real, it feels real. Unlike other films that didn’t secure the ability to use actual team names and logos (Any Given Sunday, The Replacements).

And that’s the irony of this. Davis and the league allowed the Raiders name and uniforms to be included in the film, giving it the impression of accuracy and authenticity. Which, in turn, makes the story seem accurate and authentic. Which makes it even harder to separate the truth from the fiction.

Here’s hoping Mark Davis comes up with a way to tell the true story of Al Davis. With no embellishment, fabrication, or Hollywood tricks aimed at making the story seem better than it was.

Because the story of Al Davis would be pretty damn compelling if it were indeed confined to the strict parameters of reality.

#2742. Is Dillon Brooks the Suns’ most valuable trade asset?

Stabilization. Now that we're 15 games into the season, we're starting to see some of that happen for the Phoenix Suns. They sit at 8-7, albeit as the 9th seed in the Western Conference, with plenty of basketball still to be played. We're beginning to see the vision Brian Gregory had this past offseason manifest itself on the court on a nightly basis.

And we're starting to see fewer people running to the trade machine in an attempt to fix the Phoenix Suns.

Naturally, that's part of being a fan. We recognize deficiencies and attempt to find solutions, however wild or unlikely those solutions might be. Given the tools at our disposal these days (I heart you Fanspo), it's become increasingly easy to explore potential trades. We all do it, and it's part of the fun of following a team. It's also part of the frustration, because many of the proposed solutions are completely illogical. We blindly assume another organization would gladly accept whatever trade proposal we've concocted within the confines of a trade machine.

The same could be said about a recent proposal from Fadeaway World's Siddhant Gupta. In his latest column, he made three suggestions that would send Dillon Brooks to the San Antonio Spurs. One was for Tobias Harris, with the addition of two first-round picks. The second was to send Keldon Johnson and a first-round pick to Phoenix for the Villain. The third? Exchange Brooks for Harrison Barnes, Luke Kornet, and a protected first-round pick.

What was your initial reaction to that one? Disgust? An immediate, "I'm not gonna do it"? My reaction was one I didn't expect to have. It had less to do with the proposed trade itself and more to do with the player involved. It raised a simple question: Is Dillon Brooks the Phoenix Suns' most desirable asset?

Before I dive into this whole thought exercise, I want to make one thing clear right off the bat. I have no desire for the Phoenix Suns to trade Dillon Brooks at this point in time.

He's the heartbeat of this team, the culture setter. And while he can be an inefficient shooter at times and make some poorly timed decisions, his presence is ultimately a net positive that extends well beyond the stat sheet. He helps define who this team is, and when we get an engaged version of Dillon Brooks, he lifts everyone around him. He brings out the energy and identity that make this team competitive and an absolute annoyance for the opposition.

For all those reasons, especially when you factor in his $21 million salary this season, Brooks becomes a highly desirable asset.

Look at Devin Booker. His contract is simply too much for most teams to absorb. At $57.1 million, acquiring him would require quite the haul from an opposing organization. Truth be told, as we've experienced here in Phoenix, having Devin Booker as your Batman doesn't necessarily mean you're going to take over Gotham.

Jalen Green? We've been so focused on different trade scenarios and potential returns that we've perhaps overlooked the reality of his value. Despite his elite athleticism and potential upside at 24 years old, he hasn't demonstrated that he's worth the $36.3 million he's being paid this season.

But Brooks? If you're an organization looking for a culture setter, someone who brings toughness and establishes an identity, Dillon Brooks can provide exactly that. And he does so on a contract that makes him an incredibly desirable asset.

Let's expand on this thought exercise a little further and take a longer view of what a potential Dillon Brooks trade could mean for the Phoenix Suns, without factoring in anything they might receive in return, shall we?

Brooks signed a three-year, $73 million extension this past offseason, keeping him on the books through the 2029-30 season, when he'll be making $26.1 million. As we know, the salary cap will continue to rise over the next three seasons, potentially by as much as 10% annually, with each increase compounding on the previous one. A more realistic projection is somewhere around 6%. Using that figure, the salary cap would be roughly $185 million in the final year of Brooks' contract.

The Suns are currently projected to have $145.3 million committed to salaries that season, which also happens to be the final year of Devin Booker's extension. That leaves Phoenix with approximately $40 million in cap space and five players under contract. Booker, Brooks, Collin Gillespie, Koa Peat, and Oso Ighodaro.

There's one significant factor missing from the graphic above, however. A Miles Bridges extension. Because, like it or not, it's coming. You don't surrender an unprotected 2033 first-round pick to acquire a player you ultimately have no intention of bringing back. Given Bridges' production thus far this season, I believe there's enough to justify an extension, albeit at what I would project to be a manageable number based on how this front office has operated recently.

So let's add a sixth player to the equation and hypothetically assign Bridges a $30 million salary for the 2029-30 season. There you have it. Six players under contract and approximately $10 million in cap space.

Brooks will be 33 entering that season, which by no means suggests he'll have one foot in the grave as a basketball player. However, aging players tend to become less effective and less desirable when you factor in the money they're making relative to their production, along with the increased injury risk that comes with age.

When you look at this from a bigger-picture perspective, knowing that Brooks and Bridges are somewhat duplicative in what they provide on the court, you can begin to talk yourself into the idea that the Suns' most desirable asset could help address some of their immediate deficiencies, most notably size, while also providing long-term relief on the salary cap sheet. It would create financial flexibility, open opportunities that have yet to present themselves, and make those future salary commitments easier to manage.

If you trade Brooks now for someone with only one or two years remaining on their contract, you've potentially cleared $26 million from the books in 2029-30. That gives Phoenix some financial flexibility as it prepares to enter the final season before Bradley Beal's dead money finally disappears. (Dear Lord, it still won't be off the books by then?! Nope. Not until the summer of 2031!)

In short, you're cleaning up the books in preparation for a time when the Suns will finally have money available to make some moves. You're positioning yourself to strike when the right opportunity presents itself.

Who could be available in free agency that summer? Luka Doncic. Anthony Edwards. Mikal Bridges. Pretty much anyone drafted in 2025 who hasn't signed an extension with their respective team.

Look at a team like the Utah Jazz, who the Phoenix Suns played last night. That's a team with an abundance of size. They were without Jusuf Nurkic, Jaren Jackson Jr., Lauri Markkanen, and Kyle Filipowski, yet still had Jaxson Hayes and Mo Bamba providing quality minutes as big men who could rebound and be an annoyance on the glass. I'm not suggesting you ship Dillon Brooks off to Utah, but that's certainly a team that could use a culture setter right now. They looked like a collection of individuals rather than a cohesive unit, although what else can you expect from a team dealing with that many injuries?

But who knows? Who knows where the Phoenix Suns will be on February 8? After all, that's when Brooks becomes trade-eligible after signing his extension this past offseason, only three days before the February 11 trade deadline.

At that time, they'll be closer to getting Mark Williams back, certainly, but how much do we realistically expect him to provide in terms of rim protection when he returns? He'll be coming off a significant injury and will likely be on a minutes restriction as the organization eases him back into the rotation. They recently committed to him with an extension, and the last thing they want is to risk any long-term consequences to his health.

So as we continue playing with our trade machines, and while disappointment may exist with the production of Jalen Green, I believe Dillon Brooks is the Suns' most desirable asset.

Again, I have no desire to trade him at this point. There's plenty of basketball left to be played, and we still have a lot to learn about this team. But if you're a fan looking for ways to improve the Phoenix Suns, putting Dillon Brooks into the trade machine might be the most logical place to start. His contract, production, and presence make it much easier to understand why another organization would be interested in acquiring him. Because every team that plays the Phoenix Suns finds Dillon Brooks annoying as hell. Every one of those teams would love to have a player like him. He's the kind of guy you despise when he's wearing the opposing jersey and absolutely love when he's wearing yours.

I love Dillon Brooks about as much as I love cheesy cauliflower on Thanksgiving. And if you've never had it, you're missing out. Make it with Cheez Whiz. It's delicious. Of course, you should also know that it's one of those dishes that'll have you farting for a week. Which, come to think of it, is pretty much how I felt about that proposed trade sending Dillon Brooks to the San Antonio Spurs. Ferrrrrrrt.

The Detroit Lions have placed prized free-agent center Cade Mays on injured reserve with an ankle injury, his second stint on IR this season. In a corresponding move, the Lions re-signed corner Nick Whiteside to the active roster and have also elevated linebacker Owen Pappoe for their Week 11 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Mays signed a three-year, $25 million contract with the Lions this offseason, but he's had a difficult, injury-plagued first season. After breaking his wrist in training camp, Mays spent the first six weeks on injured reserve before finally returning to action in Week 7. In Week 8, Mays injured his ankle in the first half of the Lions game with the Vikings and could not return.

While initially deemed a "low ankle sprain," Mays was only projected to miss 1-6 weeks. With that prognosis, it wasn't surprising that he was kept on the active roster and ruled OUT for Weeks 9 and 10, as a return seemed possible in the coming weeks. However, now that he has been placed on injured reserve, he must miss the next four games (Weeks 11-14) and is not eligible to return to the active roster until Week 15 (ironically against the Vikings) at the earliest. If his ankle injury is the "high" variety, his season could already be over, but we'll need to wait for an update from coach Dan Campbell before we know more.

With Mays now out for the foreseeable future, the Lions will continue to lean on Juice Scruggs, who has been terrific as an injury replacement. Scruggs is having a career year in Detroit and looks like a perfect fit for the system and culture. Behind Scruggs on the depth chart is Seth McLaughlin, who has only seen time this season in garbage-time/clock-killing situations and on special teams.

#2736. Lakers coach’s halftime message paid off vs Kings: ‘He lit me up’

With his team lacking the requisite toughness and energy during the first half of Friday's matchup against the Kings, Lakers coach JJ Redick delivered a different kind of halftime message.

And he did so in a way he hadn't done that much during the team's first 16 regular-season games, which they won 13 of.

Los Angeles Lakers coach JJ Redick had a passionate message to deliver to his team during halftime. AP Photo/Caroline Brehman

"I feel I did a decent job of regulating at halftime," Redick said. "They may have a differing opinion of that. Can't repeat every word I used. The main message was, 'We've got to be tougher, we've got to bring a little bit of energy.'"

The level of intensity that Redick brought to the locker room was nothing new for Luka Dončić after having played for Redick over 1 ½ years.

"I mean he yells, but I'm used to it," Dončić said.

But the Slovenian superstar felt that Redick's methods were necessary after the Lakers trailed by eight points to a one-win Kings team that had lost its previous seven games.

"Got us all fired up," Dončić said. "Sometimes you get to yell."

The Lakers responded to Redick's message, winning the second half 52-42 to beat the Kings 106-104 and avoid losing consecutive games for the first time this season.

The team's starting center, Walker Kessler, was among the players who took Redick's message to heart.

Kessler, who recorded a points-rebounds double-double in the previous six games and 10 of the previous 11, had just one rebound and four fouls to go with six points at halftime.

"He lit me up a little bit, rightfully so," Kessler said. "But it was constructive. He was like, 'I know you can do this. Do it.'"

Walker Kessler responded well to JJ Redick's halftime message. Getty Images

Kessler had team highs of nine points and six rebounds after halftime.

His biggest blemish in the final two quarters was missing a pair of late free throws that would've haunted the 7-foot-1 big man and the Lakers had Zach LaVine's buzzer-beating 3-point attempt converted.

But he also had one of the biggest highlights of the second half when he made his first 3-pointer of the season, a pull-up from the left corner to give the Lakers a one-point lead early in the fourth quarter.

"I wasn't playing [physically]," Kessler said of Redick's message to him. "I wasn't going up to dunk the ball. I was missing some more touches around the rim. And then defensively, being undisciplined. Jumping at stuff I don't need to jump at. He definitely lit into me. It was good. I needed it. That's what makes a good coach. Knowing when guys need that and when guys don't."

And it was clear the Lakers not only needed the message Redick delivered but also appreciated how it was delivered after not playing their best basketball over the last week to kick off the four-game homestand that ends Monday against the Jazz.

"At the core of everything that all of our coaches say, and JJ especially, they just speak to the truth of what's happening on the court," Matisse Thybulle said. "And if it needs to be said passionately, that's the message. That's how he needs to get it across, and that's what he does.

"But ultimately, JJ doesn't really mince his words, and he doesn't play games. He really gets to the point, and I think as players, we all really appreciate that. And like he understands, and we understand where he's coming from because he's been in our shoes as well."

#2732. Montverde Madness in Michigan, as Scottie and ‘Em take down the Pistons

The Raptors needed a win last night, like a person dying of thirst needs a beverage. As the adage goes, you can lead a horse to water, but you can't make them drink; and if you're Scottie Barnes, you can lead the Raptors to a win, even if you're playing without RJ Barrett and Collin Murray-Boyles.

In a game that came down to the wire, Scottie Barnes took over in clutch time, taking the ball to the bucket and dropping it in to put the Raptors up 103-102 over the team that's currently third in the Eastern Conference. A Cade Cunningham pass that was picked off by Allen Graves got the Raptors a crucial possession that resulted in them getting two free throws from Immanuel Quickley.

This forced a three from Detroit to stay alive, giving Scottie Barnes the game-winning contest over Kevin Huerter, letting Toronto seal the game, 105-102. While the first win against the Chicago Bulls came easier and let the Raptors make their mark on the NBA, this win was a life vest for Raptors fans, showing the masses what this team can do, even when down numerous crucial pieces.

The drafting of Collin-Murray Boyles and Allen Graves in back to back years felt like asking for clones of Scottie Barnes on the Raptors, and with Boyles sitting out tonight's game on concussion protocol, the rookie had his chance to put his stamp on the game, and that, he did. The rookie was the team's second leading scorer after Scottie, posting 20 points and 10 boards, career highs in both, as he stepped into the starting role. Deadly from three, the forward hit two treys for the Raptors.

Cade Cunningham had kind words for Barnes after the game, reminiscing that "that's my brother, we had English class together," while praising his development into an all-around offensive talent. Indeed, Cunningham and Barnes were teammates and classmates in high school, part of the legendary 2019-2020 Montverde Academy basketball roster. "Cade and 'Em" have formed a crux of high school basketball discourse, with endless debate about a hypothetical matchup between them and the 2015-16 Chino Hills team, led by the Ball brothers Lonzo, LiAngelo, and LaMelo.

But, with Scottie Barnes ascending in the league, he's making Montverde proud, even if it's at the expense of perhaps their favourite son.

Barnes himself had 29 points, 5 assists, and 5 rebounds, a balanced statline that demonstrates yet again Scottie's development being far from a straight line. Holding down the fort without many of his usual primary or auxiliary scorers, Scottie gave the Raptors their first win in seven games, in what may be a signature victory for the struggling team. This may be the Raptors' most impressive win of the season, and may be the turning point for a team to rally around the ascent of Scottie and Allen Graves, riding that rocket high into the Eastern Conference standings.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2720. How social media reacted to UNC's blowout loss at UVA

The North Carolina Tar Heels made a 3-hour trip up to Charlottesville for their Saturday afternoon football game, facing Virginia in the 131st installation of the South's Oldest Rivalry.

UNC and UVA entered Saturday with five wins apiece, giving this ACC rivalry showdown more stakes than usual. The winner clinches bowl eligibility, while the loser needs Thanksgiving weekend to decide its fate.

Despite totaling nearly 600 yards of offense, North Carolina played one of its worst games this season in a blowout, 41-24 loss.

The Tar Heels (5-6, 2-5 ACC) couldn't stop Virginia's (6-5, 4-4 ACC) offense, which scored five touchdowns and racked up 446 yards. Cavaliers quarterback Beau Pribula, who previously surpassed the 200-yard passing mark only twice in a game this season, enjoyed his best outing with a season-high 297 yards and four passing touchdowns. UVA running back Jekail Middlebrook caught five passes for 140 yards and a score, while Da'Shawn Martin, Xavier Brown, Dakota Twitty and Solomon Beebe (rushing touchdown) also found the end zone.

UNC entered Saturday as the ACC's least penalized team, but committed 11 penalties for 82 yards against Virginia. North Carolina failed to convert fourth downs on consecutive drives, while Rece Verhoff missed a pair of field goals, which proved to be the four largest mistakes Saturday afternoon.

Billy Edwards took pre-game first team reps for the Tar Heels, but true freshman Travis Burgess thrived in his first career start instead. Between a pair of interceptions, Burgess totaled 460 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns, extending several drives with his legs. Burgess found an immediate connection with Jordan Shipp, connecting with UNC's leading pass-catcher for nine completions and 149 yards.

#2719. Rob Pelinka on Lakers: 'We’ll be active at the trade deadline'

The Los Angeles Lakers sit on top of the Western Conference at 14-3, with the third-best offense in the NBA — behind an MVP-level start to the season from Luka Doncic — and a solid defense. Walker Kessler has been exactly what the Lakers hoped for as a big in the paint, and their moves for role players that better fit around Doncic — Matisse Thybulle, Sandro Mamukelashvili, Quentin Grimes, Quentin Grimes — have largely worked out.

Lakers general manager Rob Pelinka has seen it, too, and thinks this team has a deep playoff run in them. Which is why he said in an interview on the Lakers pregame show that the team would be "active" at the trade deadline (hat tip Real GM).

"We'll be active at the trade deadline to shore up things that we see. We think this team has a real chance to make a run, so we want to give the group as much talent as we can. Don't want to get too far over our skis with a hot start, because you don't want to get big-headed, but clearly the way it's gone so far, it's been great, and we hope it continues."

Active is a broad term. The Lakers will be active talking to teams, whether they make a deal will depend on the players available, and the price.

The Lakers' most critical need is to improve at backup center behind Kessler. Kevon Looney has largely fallen out of the rotation, leaving the Lakers playing small ball with Sandro Mamukelashvili or Jarred Vanderbilt at the five, or leaning into two-way big Carson Cooper. There may be better options available.

The Lakers don't have draft picks of note to trade, but they have players, and while they are hard-capped at the first apron, they are a little more than $8 million below that line and have room to work.

Henderson was placed on injured reserve ahead of Week 10 and will miss the next four games, at minimum.

Impact: Recent reports indicate Darnold could return following the team's Week 11 bye.

Holani is week-to-week with an MCL sprain as of Week 11.

#2715. CeeDee Lamb fined $23,882 for block the league used as a highlight

When Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb made a downfield block on a George Pickens touchdown catch Sunday against the 49ers, the league’s website was so impressed that the highlight video on NFL.com emphasized Lamb’s block over Pickens’ touchdown.

“Can’t-Miss Play: CeeDee Lamb’s HUGE block springs Pickens free for 39-yard TD,” the caption on the highlight video says.

Calling the play on Fox, Tom Brady praised Lamb, immediately recognizing it as a great downfield block.

But the league’s disciplinary process didn’t think it was so great. Lamb has been fined $23,882 for what the NFL deemed “Unnecessary Roughness: Use of the helmet.”

Lamb confirmed to reporters on Thursday that he had been informed he was getting fined, but he insisted he didn’t make contact with his helmet and found it frustrating that receivers take hits routinely but get fined when they make one.

“I can block, and I’m real good at doing things like that, but I get fined,” Lamb said. “I never touched him with my helmet. . . . I guess as a receiver, we can get hit, but can’t deliver the punishment.”

Lamb will surely appeal the fine for what looked, both to the league’s website and the league’s all-time greatest player, like a good block.

#2714. Eagles Urged to Trade Up for Best WR Prospect in 25 Years

The Philadelphia Eagles grabbed a wide receiver in the 1st round of the 2026 NFL Draft, landing USC's Makai Lemon at No. 23 overall. That doesn't mean he has to be their future at the position.

That player will be in the 2027 NFL Draft: Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith. He's on track to become the first wide receiver taken with the No. 1 overall pick since the New York Jets selected USC's Keyshawn Johnson with the top pick in the 1996 NFL Draft.

Bleacher Report's Brent Sobleski put the Eagles at the top of his list of teams that should do whatever it takes to trade up for Smith — a deal that could easily package 1st-round picks with Lemon to make it happen.

The Eagles are 2-7 and have lost 7 straight games. If the draft were tomorrow, they would have the No. 5 overall pick.

"Calvin Johnson, AJ Green, Julio Jones and Ja'Marr Chase are the best wide receiver prospects over the last 25 years," Sobleski wrote on Saturday. "None of them were the No. 1 overall pick in their respective draft classes. Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith is on par with all four as a prospect and possibly even better. NFL teams should be falling over themselves to try to acquire his services … Smith can completely change the complexion of the Eagles' roster, especially on offense. What the team lost when it traded AJ Brown can be reinserted with a younger, more explosive version. Thus, a trio of Jeremiah Smith, DeVonta Smith and Lemon will be extremely difficult to defend, with each placed in specific roles to maximize their skill sets."

"This is a once-in-a-lifetime WR prospect right here," Touchdown Tube wrote on its official Instagram account.

Smith, 6-foot-4 and 223 pounds, is currently the projected No. 1 overall pick in the latest mock drafts from both Bleacher Report and ESPN.

From B/R: "Smith is a proven, game-changing wide receiver with a special blend of size, speed and strength. The 6'4″, 225-pound target plays through contact, using physical route-running to shed handsy defenders. With excellent acceleration and long speed, Smith glides past corners and threatens the defense vertically. The Ohio State receiver is an NFL WR1 from Day 1 and should be peppered with targets early and often."

Three AFC teams are 1-8 headed into Week 11 and all neck-and-neck for the No. 1 overall pick — the Miami Dolphins, Los Angeles Chargers and Tennessee Titans.

ESPN's Jordan Reid has Smith going to the Titans at No. 1 in his latest mock draft.

"Smith is the best player in this draft, and as the first wide receiver to go No. 1 since 1996 (Keyshawn Johnson), he would allow the Titans to continue to build around quarterback Cam Ward, the No. 1 pick of the 2025 draft," Reid wrote on November 18. "How special is Smith? He has drawn comparisons to some of the best wideouts of the past quarter century — including Calvin Johnson, Larry Fitzgerald and Julio Jones — by NFL scouts."

#2711. Brad Stevens talks Mitchell Robinson, Celtics’ start, and more

SACRAMENTO — Brad Stevens took a lot of heat this offseason for pulling the trigger on the trade that sent Jaylen Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers and ended a near-decade-long partnership with Jayson Tatum.

And, though it's too soon to tell, the Celtics are 11-4, have the second-best net rating in the NBA, the second-best defense, and the sixth-best offense. Paul George, the team's biggest offseason acqusition, has been generally awesome. The team's significant depth has been on full display regularly.

Still, Stevens said it's too soon to judge who this team really is, and that he normally waits until mid-December to make those kinds of evaluations.

"I've been encouraged by a lot of things," Stevens said. "I think we've still got a lot to figure out to be the best version of ourselves. But usually, I'm probably another couple of weeks or a month away from getting too deep into, okay, this is who we really are. Yet, I think we have played some good basketball. We've shown ourselves capable of it. We've gotten good play from a lot of different guys, and the team has really tried to buy in, I think, well, to what the coaches are asking them to do on both sides of the ball."

Paul George has been one of the brightest spots of the Celtics' early-season success. George has been tremendous defensively, and he's also averaging 19.9 points, 5.5 rebounds, and 3.7 assists per game, while shooting 46.5% from the field and 42.3% from three. He's had two games with at least 35 points and has been one of the team's most reliable defenders.

"Paul's been a good fit," Stevens said. "Paul's a really good player…. You don't come with those accolades if you're not able to impact the game. Everybody talks about what he can do on offense, and I think the minute he stepped on the court with our guys defensively, our guys, a lot of them were kind of taken aback, even though playing against him all these years, with how good he is, how active he is, how smart he is, how aware he is, and he's just really had a good impact on the group. He's just been a joy to be around. He's been great."

The Celtics' other marquee offseason acquisition, Mitchell Robinson, hasn't transitioned as seamlessly as George. Robinson has the worst on-off rating on the Celtics at -30.1 (that number measures the difference in net rating when a player is on the floor versus off of it). The historically prolific rebounder is also averaging the fewest rebounds per game (5.4) of his career.

"You can tell it's obviously a transition for him, and that's not all that atypical for guys, and so again, it's so early that we'll see how this all plays out," Stevens said. "But I trust that what he does when he's at his best will translate because it always has, right? And I think that getting him to the rim on both sides of the floor, getting him to be in that area where he can be most impactful, [is] something that we'll continue to work on — continue to put him in position where, hopefully, he can soar with his strengths."

Then, there's rookie Chris Cenac Jr., who began the year with the Maine Celtics but has found himself in the Celtics' rotation over the past two games. Cenac, who was drafted 27th overall, tallied 6 points and 6 rebounds in 17 minutes in the Celtics' loss to the Nuggets on Wednesday night.

"He's been solid," Stevens said. "I'm really encouraged. I really like him. I think he's got a great work ethic. He's obviously got physical tools. He's got a good mind for the game. He's gonna be good, right? I do think that with each step, there are different expectations. So he's in that honeymoon phase of, well, he did one good thing and it looks awesome, and wow. And then your expectations grow and grow, and it's just like we've seen with Jordan and Hugo and Baylor. Once you taste it, once you get a little feeling, then the expectation is to be even better, and we see that all the way up and down our roster. All of our guys, for the most part, have been through that. But I'm encouraged by the start. It's hard not to be, and I think the other part of it is he does have the physical ability to continue to raise his level in big moments."

One of the other interesting aspects of the roster is the logjam at the wing position; Sam Hauser (20.3 minutes), Baylor Scheierman (19.4 minutes), Jordan Walsh (15.7 minutes), and Hugo Gonzalez (12.9 minutes) have all seen significant minutes, but no one player in that group has pulled away to play the majority of the minutes.

Each brings something different to the table; Hauser (46.8% from three) and Scheierman (42.2% from three) have been the biggest threats from beyond the arc, while Gonzalez (7.1 rebounds/36 minutes) has been the best rebounder of the bunch. From the wings, Walsh has probably been the team's best on-ball defender and its most consistent starter, with 10 starts in 15 games.

But the players have seemed interchangeable at times, and no one has clearly emerged as the best player in the pack.

"I said at the start of the year, the biggest challenge for the coaching staff is the wing differentiation," Stevens said. "That's been the hardest part, and I think they've managed it beautifully, because nobody has really differentiated themselves, and they're all good players. And so that's just kind of the hard part about having depth, which in this league you need now. It's really important, but it also comes with the challenges of — not everybody's going to get exactly what they want on every given night. Is it easier to have seven or eight guys that you know are going to play every night? Yeah, until two of them get hurt, then you're in trouble, right? And so that's part of the challenge in this day and age with how the league is going and how hard it is to play the full 82, and certainly game to game with what's required on both ends."

As the team continues to improve on both ends, Stevens is generally encouraged by what he's seen.

"One of the things that this group really has is a lot of feel for how to play, and you see that when we're at our very best on both ends: the reaction, the reads, the ability to play off one another, the ability to cover for one another on the defensive end," Stevens said. "I think that those are things that, as the season goes on, we should continue to benefit from, to be able to grow, kind of however Joe and the staff want us to play throughout that given stretch, and ultimately to be the best that we can be."

#2709. Chiefs elevate 2 practice squad players for Week 11

Ahead of Week 11's home matchup against the Arizona Cardinals, the Kansas City Chiefs announced a pair of practice squad elevations for the contest.

Running back Nate Carter and center Pete Nygra will get the nod on Sunday. As elevated players, they will immediately revert to the practice squad after the game.

Second-year pro Carter made his Chiefs debut last week against the Atlanta Falcons as star running back Kenneth Walker sat with a groin injury. He carried the ball twice for six yards in relief of rookie Emmett Johnson, who finished the game with 171 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns. Walker is ruled out again, but rookie running back Jadyn Ott has no game status after missing Week 10 with a hamstring injury. Assuming Ott is available to spell Johnson, Carter may only be an emergency option against Arizona.

Nygra signed with Kansas City in April as an undrafted free agent out of Louisville. He has been a member of the practice squad the entire season after failing to make the final roster. Sunday will make Nygra's NFL debut.

Earlier this week, longtime Chiefs center — and current Sports Radio 810 WHB host — Tim Grunhard suggested that third-year pro Hunter Nourzad would start at right guard with starter Trey Smith in concussion protocol. Over three seasons, the Chiefs have seemed to view Nourzad as a center-specific backup while frequently bringing him in for six offensive lineman formations.

Having another center in Nygra available would suggests merit to Grunhard's report that Nourzad — and not Mike Caliendo — may truly get the start on Sunday.

Also on Saturday, the Cardinals downgraded rookie quarterback Carson Beck to out with back spasms before departing to Kansas City. Beck had been listed as questionable on Friday after missing practice. 40-year-old Josh Johnson will officially start at quarterback against Kansas City on Sunday.

Arizona also elevated veteran wideout Zay Jones from their practice squad.

#2708. Australia hold on for narrow win against Wales

Tries: Lake 2, Murray, Elias Cons: Costelow 3

Tries: Tupou, Paenga-Amosa, Jorgensen, Ikitau Cons: Lonergan 2, Gordon Pens: Gordon

Wales could not emulate their famous victory against New Zealand as Australia claimed the Nations Championship spoils in Cardiff.

The Wallabies ended a four-match losing run thanks to tries from hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa, prop Taniela Tupou, wing Max Jorgensen and centre Len Ikitau, while fly-half Carter Gordon kicked a late penalty.

Wales captain Dewi Lake scored two tries, while full-back Blair Murray also crossed following a superb assist by wing Louis Rees-Zammit.

Replacement hooker Ryan Elias grabbed a late try but Australia held on for victory as Wales paid the price for not capitalising on attacking chances.

Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere section and will play Japan at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Saturday (13:10 GMT).

Australia finished third in the southern hemisphere table and play Ireland on Friday (20:10 GMT).

After all the hysteria and celebrations to mark a first victory against the All Blacks in 73 years, the attention turned towards whether Wales could back it up against Australia.

There was a vibrancy on the streets of Cardiff before the game not seen for a while, which reflected in the crowd.

After crowds of 52,425 against Japan and 55,152 against New Zealand, the 66,307 attendance against Australia was the highest of the autumn.

The All Blacks win proved instrumental in a surge of tickets sold for a 20:10 GMT kick-off, the latest for a Wales rugby home game at the Principality Stadium.

Head coach Steve Tandy made four changes to revert to the side that beat Japan with flanker James Botham the most notable absentee following his player-of-the-match against New Zealand.

Botham was expecting the birth of his first child this week but Tandy stated his omission was for rugby reasons with Cardiff colleague Alex Mann replacing him.

Fit-again number eight Aaron Wainwright replaced Taine Basham, while lock Ben Carter and wing Josh Adams returned for Adam Beard and Gabriel Hamer-Webb.

Australia had freshened things up with five forward changes as flanker Carlo Tizzano, lock Tom Hooper and the front-row trio of Isaac Kailea, Paenga-Amosa and Tupou came in.

Wales lost centre Max Llewellyn inside two minutes to a yellow card for a high tackle on Wallabies full-back Tom Wright.

Wallabies had plenty of early possession against 14 players but the home defence comfortably dealt with the attack.

Mann was caught with some friendly fire by a finger in the eye from team-mate Carter but continued despite appearing to have vision issues.

Rees-Zammit almost squeezed into the corner but just failed to ground the ball under pressure from Gordon, before Lake was held up over the Australia line.

Mann, despite his eye seeming to be closing, was still able to force a turnover penalty but Wales were guilty of early handling errors.

After Wales won a scrum penalty, the officials then either missed Tupou striking Mann with a body jab, or deemed it did not warrant further action.

Tupou stayed on the field to open the scoring in the 21st minute as he evaded Llewellyn's tackle to cross for an unconverted try.

Wales captain Dewi Lake has now scored 12 tries in 37 internationals [Huw Evans Picture Agency]

Wales retaliated quickly with Morgan breaking away and feeding scrum-half Tomos Williams, who was held up by superb visiting defence.

There were important turnover penalties from Tizzano and Tupou who benefitted from a huge tackle from Australia captain Harry Wilson on opposite number Wainwright.

The hosts held the upper hand in the first-half aerial battle but Wales were not as clinical as they were against New Zealand.

Australia centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii gained an intercept before being hauled down by Rees-Zammit, who conceded a penalty.

Wallabies demonstrated a more ruthless approach as Paenga-Amosa was driven over.

Mann continued to wind up the Australia forwards, which helped gain 10 metres for dissent, but Wales continued to waste chances as an attacking line-out was stolen.

Morgan was a Wales carrying colossus in the first half with a series of impressive bursts and the home side finally gained a reward in the 40th minute when Lake dived over with Costelow converting.

Australia led 12-7 at half-time with Wales having an on-pitch huddle before heading to their changing room.

Suaalii towered over Murray to take an early second-half attacking high ball but Wallabies were denied a try by a brilliant Morgan turnover.

Australia scrum-half Lonergan missed a penalty before Wallabies' second-half aerial dominance was rewarded when Jorgensen rose above Adams before finishing off the move to score.

Wales brought on a raft of replacements, including an early introduction for scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams.

The changes worked when Lake was driven over for his second score before Wales followed up with a magical try.

Rees-Zammit was the architect with a stunning outside break before feeding Adams who provided the try-scoring pass to Murray.

Costelow's conversion gave Wales the lead for the first time.

Australia brought on experienced forward replacements with Fraser McReight and Angus Bell making immediate impacts.

Prop Allan Alaalatoa appeared to have scored on his 99th international, but it was ruled out following a knock-on by replacement scrum-half Kalani Thomas.

The Wallabies wave continued with Wales duo Eddie James and Archie Griffin producing impressive tackles before Ikitau restored the visitors' lead.

Morgan left the field for a head injury assessment (HIA) to be replaced by Kane James, who was in tears when the anthem was played as he marked his first Wales appearance in Cardiff.

Fellow replacement Louie Hennessey knocked on to give Australia an attacking platform before Wainwright conceded a penalty which Carter kicked to take the Wallabies two scores clear.

Morgan returned and Wales responded as they battered the Australia line with Wilson shown a yellow card.

Elias was driven over to secure two losing bonus-points and set up a grandstand finale, but Wallabies held on for a vital victory for head coach Les Kiss.

Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Adams; Costelow, T Williams; Smith, Lake (capt), Griffin, Jenkins, Carter, Mann, Morgan, Wainwright.

Replacements: Elias, G Thomas, Lewis, Plumtree, K James, Morgan-Williams, Hawkins, Hennessey.

Australia: Wright; Jorgensen, Suaalii, Ikitau, Potter; Gorden, Lonergan; Kailea, Paenga-Amosa, Tupou, Canham, Hooper, Valetini, Tizzano, Wilson (capt).

Replacements: Pollard, Bell, Alaalatoa, Williams, McReight, Thomas, Donaldson, Daugunu.

Assistant referees: Karl Dickson (England) & Jeremy Rozier (France).

Television match official (TMO): Eric Gauzins (France).

Foul play review officer (FPRO): Andrew Jackson (RFU).

#2706. Sixers get lucky with their 14th win as Herro can’t get off game-tying three in time

The Sixers just outlasted the Milwaukee Bucks by a literal second, hanging on to win 132-129 Saturday afternoon, notching their fifth win in a row and improving to 14-3 on the season.

Joel Embiid did a lot to make up for a subpar shooting night, finishing with a team-high 26 points, a season-high 17 rebounds, and nine assists shooting 7-of-17 from the floor. After missing last game with a foot sprain, Tyrese Maxey had one of his quietest games of the year finishing with 17 points on 4-of-11 shooting.

LeBron James played quarterback for much of the day, finishing with 21 points, six rebounds and six assists going 9-of-14. VJ Edgecombe shot 5-of-12 from the floor to finish with 16 points with three rebounds and six assists. Tyler Herro led all scorers with 50 but his three to tie the game just didn't beat the buzzer.

Jaylen Brown and Dean Wade missed their second straight game, both dealing with hamstring strains, along with Adem Bona, who's missed the last eight. Milwaukee was without Ousmane Dieng.

The Sixers got two of their easiest buckets all season to open the game off of cuts. James went down the baseline and Edgecombe flashed to the middle of the paint. Their pull-up jump shooting was a different story early. Embiid even had a midrange blocked by Myles Turner as the Sixers struggled to capitalize on a 1-of-8 start for the Bucks.

Embiid also had a layup attempt blocked by Turner as he started the game 0-of-4 from the field. His other two jumpers falling just off the rim. On the other end the Sixers allowed two offensive rebounds to turn into second-chance points as the Bucks' offense was the first to find a rhythm.

The Sixers' offense settled in after an early timeout from Nick Nurse. They got a couple of open threes from Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Edgecombe broke Turner down off the dribble, and LeBron opened up plenty of space on a drive to hit Embiid with a lob. James made a great one-handed pass cross court to find KCP in the corner a few possessions later but the three rimmed out. KCP and Embiid also both missed fast break layups that halted a run.

Jabari Walker checked in next to Embiid at the four like he has in recent games and was rewarded for cutting by Embiid shortly after checking in. Dominick Barlow made his season debut a few minutes later, relieving Embiid. Labaron Philon Jr. remained in the rotation and picked up a floater, but also fouled Herro attempting a three right before the quarter ended. Herro made all three to give the Bucks a one-point lead after one.

Barlow's first big impact was tipping back a missed Maxey floater for Philly's first points of the second. On the next possession he ran down the floor to catch a lob after LeBron had just about singlehandedly created. It wasn't all perfect — the Bucks scored six straight field goals in the paint, but it was a fine first shift back for Barlow.

LeBron was easily the best player on the floor for the Sixers. His ability to lead people open gave them a lot of easy baskets that were much needed for an offense struggling to hit jumpers. They were also struggling to finish off defensive possessions as the Bucks picked up their 10th second-chance point on eight offensive rebounds.

Maxey got downhill quick and drew a foul which gave Nurse a chance to use a timeout. Coming out of that break, it seemed like there was an ever bigger focus to run quickly, whether if it was after a make or a miss. After Maxey zoomed through for a layup, Edgecombe got down the floor twice, setting up Walker and Embiid for buckets at the rim.

It was weird because the Sixers weren't playing great defense by any means, but the Bucks still had a bunch of airballs in the first half, more than any NBA team should. The misses the Sixers got were ugly, but they hadn't made life hard on Herro at all — he was able to get to just about every spot on the floor.

The first trouble Herro ran into all night was when he tried to contest an Embiid dunk in transition and took a shot to the face while unsuccessfully doing so. The dunk seemed to finally get Embiid going as he was able to bully past Turner for an and-1 after trying all half to do so. That capped off an 8-0 run that gave the Sixers a one-point lead at the break.

Sandwiched in between a pair of free throws from Maxey and Embiid, LeBron got to the basket for another big dunk. A few possessoins later, Embiid finally got a midrange to go over Turner. Not much had changed defensively as the Bucks scored on their first four possessions of the second half.

The Sixers definitley got more comfortable in their half court offense as the game went on. After paint buckets from Maxey and Edgecombe, KCP knocked a three to give the Sixers a lead they were able to hang on to for more than one possession. Aside from losing Herro once on the perimeter as they came down the floor, the defense had improved as well. Embiid had started to do a good job of finishing possessions as he passed his season high in rebounds.

Simons and KCP were the only Sixers who had made a three to this point in the game, so it was a good thing they were both feeling it. Simons ripped eight straight points to give the Sixers their first double-digit lead of the night.

Embiid threw a nice one-handed pass into the corner for Edgecombe who finally became the third Sixer of the night to hit a three. Edgecombe tried to run quickly off a made free throw, but had his layup attempt blocked by Kel'el Ware. Simons got a chance for yet another buzzer-beater, but his midrange attempt didn't fall, neither did Embiid's humorous attempt to get a shot off with 0.2 seconds remaining. The Sixers held a six-point lead after the third.

Barlow did get up a corner three in his first shift and airballed it pretty bad. He got another chance in his second shift and got plenty of arc to bury it this time. LeBron found him from the high-post for a layup on the next possession to prompt an early Bucks timeout.

Shortly after James found Barlow cutting to the basket again and hit him for the layup, drawing a foul in the process. The Sixers lost their grip on Herro coming out of the timeout though, letting him get to the basket a couple of times. The Sixers nearly forced a turnover, but left AJ Green open in the process, who was able to hit a three to cut it back to a one-possession game.

After calling a timeout, the Sixers put the ball in LeBron's hands, who was able to back in his way in for a bucket, putting back his own missed floater. Thanks to another offensive rebound from Barlow on the next possession, Maxey was able to scoot to the basket for two more. James bullied his way for two more baskets, drawing a foul on one, to restore order a bit.

Milwaukee was able to respond with a basket nearly every time the Sixers scored a big one, but they couldn't get stops with LeBron locked in. They ran the same play just about every time down the floor, having Maxey come up to screen for LeBron while Embiid had the ball, and it got LeBron open every time.

Herro missed an open floater down six with a minute, which seemed like it would put the Bucks away for good. Not only did Embiid come up empty on both Sixers possessions, but the Bucks scored quick off those misses, cutting it back down to two with 12 seconds left. The Sixers hurried to beat the Bucks down the floor and Turner had to foul Embiid, picking up his sixth of the game. Embiid buried both free throws, but Brayden Burries stepped back into the corner, burying the open three to cut it to one with 4.8 to go.

Embiid went way into the backcourt on the inbound to take three seconds off the clock before being fouled. It was hard to tell from press row, but he definitely stepped out of bounds running towards the sideline and got lucky the refs missed it. He made both free throws to make it a three-point game with 1.5 seconds left and the Bucks had one timeout left to advance. The Sixers put Barlow in for Embiid. The Bucks sent Herro down the other end of the court who took a dribble before getting his three up. He buried the shot, silencing the crowd, but replay showed that he just didn't get it off in time, making the Sixers very lucky to escape this one in regulation.

#2705. Cowboys vs Titans: Writer predictions for Week 11

Dallas gets one of its best opportunities of the season to steady things after the 46-40 loss to San Francisco. Tennessee is 1-8 and ranks near the bottom of the league on both sides of the ball. Dallas should be the better team here, but after giving up 584 yards last week, the defense still has something to prove.

Tennessee should lean heavily on Tony Pollard. The former Cowboy has 628 rushing yards and six touchdowns, and Dallas has just been gashed for 214 yards on the ground by San Francisco. If the Titans can get Pollard moving early, it takes pressure off Cam Ward and gives Tennessee a chance to control the tempo.

Dallas has to make Ward win this game through the air. Tennessee ranks near the bottom of the league in scoring and total offense, while Ward has been inconsistent despite showing flashes. The Cowboys need to contain Pollard, keep Ward in the pocket and force long third downs. With Tennessee also dealing with injuries at receiver, Dallas should have the advantage if it avoids the missed tackles and busted assignments that hurt so badly last week.

This is where Dallas should take control. Tennessee owns the league's worst pass defense, while Dak Prescott is playing some of his best football and just threw five touchdowns against San Francisco. With CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens both capable of taking over a game, Dallas should attack downfield rather than becoming too conservative.

Javonte Williams still needs enough work to keep Tennessee honest, but this matchup belongs in Prescott's hands. The Titans can create turnovers, so Dallas cannot get careless, but if the offensive line protects well there should be favourable matchups across the field all afternoon.

The Cowboys should have too much firepower for Tennessee. If Dallas tackles better, limits Pollard and avoids gifting the Titans short fields, this is a game it should control.

Often a shakeup mid-season sees at least a temporary improvement in performance. I think that will be the case here. Cowboys 34 Titans 23

The Cowboys made a big shakeup this week by taking play-calling duties away from Christian Parker. I feel like the defense is going to try to win this game for their defensive coordinator, and it sets them up well with the Tennessee Titans coming to town.

The Titans should be a get-right game for the Cowboys on all fronts, for a team that's in desperate need of a win. Dallas should have their best performance of the season on defense and should have a strong performance on offense, leading to a 34-17 win before Thanksgiving.

The Cowboys have struggled against every team this season, good and bad. Considering the game day changes Dallas has made with the defensive play-calling duties, there is a chance Dallas finally takes care of things against a bad team early in a game instead of in the waning moments. But I won't trust it until I see it. My gut feeling tells me Dallas wins by a touchdown or less. Let's go with 31-27 Cowboys

The Cowboys are no doubt a mess, but this absolutely has to be a get-right matchup for them. With all the issues both on and off the field I don't have much confidence they'll do it, but I'm going to pick Dallas to get a win. Give me the Cowboys, 33-23.

To lose this one would bring shame to the game for Dallas. Sure, things are rough right now for the Cowboys after last week, and to lose this one would be a massive shock to all of Cowboys Nation. Confidence is best described as positive, but skidish. Cowboys win 31-17.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2703. LSU loses safety Ty Benefield for targeting, ejected vs. Tennessee football

Tennessee football caught a couple of major breaks on its final drive of the first half vs. LSU on Nov. 20. Two Tigers defensive penalties set up the go-ahead score that put the Vols ahead at halftime.

With 26 seconds left in the second quarter and Tennessee trailing 6-3, starting LSU safety Ty Benefield was flagged for targeting. His penalty proved to be a major lift for a Vols offense that was struggling to get into gear at that point.

Benefield was going for a tackle on Tennessee tight end DaSaahn Brame as he attempted to spin for a first down at the LSU 20-yard line. Benefield lowered his head and put the crown of his helmet right into Brame's midsection. After a review, officials ruled it was indeed targeting and ejected Benefield from the game.

In addition to costing the Tigers one of their best defensive players, the penalty moved Tennessee up to the two yard line. Two plays later, quarterback George MacIntyre connected with Brame for a two-yard touchdown reception, that gave the Vols a 10-6 lead at halftime.

Benefield, a transfer from Boise State, had made 49 tackles and 2 interceptions going into the Tennessee game. He had made a team-leading eight tackles, to go along with a sack, a forced fumble and pass defended, against the Vols before being ejected.

Stephen Thompson covers Tennessee Volunteers men's basketball. Email him at stephen.thompson@knoxnews.com and follow him on X @stephenethom.

#2701. Ime Udoka calls Rockets 'mentally fragile' after loss to Nuggets

After a 7-1 start to the season, the Rockets have gone 5-4 — including a loss to Denver on Friday night — with the 13th-ranked defense in the NBA.

After that loss to the Nuggets, Rockets coach Ime Udoka called his team "mentally fragile" and had more to say (quote via Varun Shankar of the Houston Chronicle).

"There's no effort or any attention to detail on the defensive end at all.... They had four 30-point quarters... you're not going to win anything and that just shows a lack of effort, attention to detail or fight on that end. And so, doesn't really matter what we did offensively. Play that poorly, you're not going to win any games."

It seems a little early in the season to call your team soft, but Udoka is an old-school, defense-first, outwork-your-opponent kind of coach, and Houston's effort lately is clearly frustrating him. Also frustrating him was the fact that Nikola Jokic scored 24 points in the second half (although he has done that to a lot of teams).

Things are not dire in Houston, the Rockets had won 4-of-5 before Friday night and still sit as the No. 4 seed in the West with the second-best offense in the NBA. It's a long regular season where the Rockets can work out their defense and get it on point, this is a team that can make a deep run in the West. Which is why Udoka expects more from them than he has seen of late.

#2698. 2 49ers, CeeDee Lamb fined in Niners vs. Cowboys

The San Francisco 49ers saw two players issued fines in the aftermath of the Dallas Cowboys game last weekend as defensive backs Siran Neal and Marques Sigle were both flagged for infractions.

Neal was fined $8,639 for an unnecessary roughness penalty, stemming from a punt return in the fourth quarter, where he was flagged for a facemask. The punt had initially pinned Dallas inside the 20, but Neal's penalty on the tackle gave the Cowboys field position at their 34-yard line.

Dallas would end up going 10 plays for 66 yards and a touchdown, cutting the lead to 38-32.

Sigle was fined $6,142 for unnecessary roughness for a hit on a defenseless player. He was not flagged on the play, which came on a third-down incompletion early in the second quarter. Dallas would punt on the next play.

Those weren't the only two fines from the game. CeeDee Lamb was fined $23,882 for an illegal use of the helmet while delivering a block on Deommodore Lenoir on George Pickens's 39-yard touchdown in the second quarter that put the Cowboys up 16-10.

There was initially a flag thrown on the play, but it was picked up.

On replay, it looked like Lamb delivered a hit with his shoulder to Lenoir's shoulder on the block. He expressed frustration earlier in the week with the penalty when revealing he got fined.

"I guess as a receiver, we can get hit, but can't deliver the punishment," Lamb said, via the Dallas News's Joseph Hoyt.

The 49ers ended up winning 46-40, and are now moving on to face the Minnesota Vikings this weekend, with kickoff set for 5:20 p.m. on Sunday night in Mexico City. Meanwhile, the Cowboys will face the Tennessee Titans at home, looking to bounce back from the loss.

Tyler Herro scored a career-high 50 points Saturday, but that wasn't enough for the Milwaukee Bucks to get their second win of the season in a 132-129 defeat to the Philadelphia 76ers.

Milwaukee was deprived of an opportunity to take the lead in the closing seconds when officials missed Joel Embiid stepping out of bounds.

Rookie Brayden Burries hit a corner 3-pointer for the Bucks to cut the Sixers' lead to 130-129. After a timeout, LeBron James threw an inbounds pass to Embiid, who attempted to dribble out the clock near the Milwaukee basket. Embiid stepped out of bounds at the baseline with his left foot, but the officials did not call the turnover and Herro was forced to foul.

The Bucks could not challenge the non-call because they were out of replay challenges.

Embiid made his two free throws to put Philadelphia ahead by 3, but the Bucks still had 1.5 seconds remaining to try for a tying basket.

Herro received the inbounds pass from Kyle Kuzma at the top of the arc and took one dribble to break free from VJ Edgecombe. Shooting from the right elbow, Herro's 3-pointer went in. However, the shot left his hand after the buzzer.

The eighth-year guard shot 15 for 23 from the floor, including 7 of 13 on 3-pointers. Herro also hit all 11 of his free throws, adding 11 rebounds and seven assists. Burries finished with 26 points off the bench with 8 rebounds and four assists. Kuzma was the third Bucks player to reach double figures, scoring 12 with five boards.

Herro's previous career-high was 41 points, reached in a December 2022 win over the Houston Rockets while he was with the Miami Heat.

Milwaukee lost its 13th consecutive game to drop to 1-16 on the season, the worst mark in the NBA. The Bucks' only win came nearly a month ago on Oct. 26, a 110-102 victory over the Indiana Pacers. Up next for them is the Toronto Raptors (6-10) at home on Monday.

The 76ers improved to 14-3 with the win, tying the Los Angeles Lakers for the NBA's top record. Philadelphia has won five consecutive games and next faces the Portland Trail Blazers (10-5) on Monday.

#2688. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class is ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. We've seen and will continue to see predictions that he's going to land a deal of around 8-10 years and topping $400 million. The knee-jerk reaction to such prognostications in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the signing team is getting a surefire ace for several years.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. If he signs an eight-year deal, it'll run through his age-37 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the team owner who ends up signing Skubal, are you sure you're really worried that he won't be productive through five, six, seven or even all eight years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 10-year, $400 million deal for this guy would be a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it would be a bargain.
